messages.content: question regarding MOA for private/regulated tiers: Because we want to make sure that only the installed LLM can "touch" LP or Patient data, do we set the installed LLM as the "router" that determines where the entered question/query should go? Meaning, if the user asks about LP/Patient stuff, it will get routed to installed LLM and anything else can go to the API model?

[System: The active model for this chat has changed to deepseek-v4-flash via provider deepseek. From this point forward, use this runtime metadata when answering questions about what model/provider is active.]

question regarding MOA for private/regulated tiers: Because we want to make sure that only the installed LLM can "touch" LP or Patient data, do we set the installed LLM as the "router" that determines where the entered question/query should go? Meaning, if the user asks about LP/Patient stuff, it will get routed to installed LLM and anything else can go to the API model?

Straight answer: **yes, the router has to be the installed LLM — but routing alone isn't what protects the data.** Here's the design:

## The rule that makes it work

**The router reads the query.** If the router were the cloud API model, the sensitive text would already be out the door before any routing happened. So the router must run locally — that part of your design is correct and non-negotiable.

But routing is only layer 1 of 3. The actual guarantee comes from the other two:

**Layer 1 — Local router (Qwen 27B).** Ingress classifies every query: sensitive (LP/Patient) → local model; general → API model. Keep the router prompt minimal and pinned so it's auditable.

**Layer 2 — Data access control (the real enforcement).** The API model must *never* have retrieval access to the LP/Patient stores — vector DB, CRM, docs, whatever. Local model is the only one that can fetch that data. So even if the router botches a classification and sends a sensitive query to the API model, the API model has **nothing to pull** — it answers from general knowledge, no exfil path. This is the "no data path" design, and it's what you'd actually defend in a BAA audit.

**Layer 3 — Sanitize what leaves.** Never forward the raw conversation history to the API model — history is the leak vector (user asks a general question right after a sensitive exchange, and the whole thread rides along). Build the API call fresh, redacted.

## Two more decisions

- **Default to local.** A false positive (keeping a general query local) costs you a few cents of GPU. A false negative (sending LP/Patient data out) is a breach. So the rule is: *only route out when confident it's non-sensitive; anything ambiguous stays on Qwen.* Regulated environments can't afford an aggressive router.
- **Deterministic pre-filter first.** Cheap regex/entity check for PHI patterns and known names (fund names, patient names) before the LLM router even fires. Catches the obvious cases for free, then the model handles the fuzzy ones.

## One naming flag

This isn't really MOA (mixture of agents). MoA proper fans the same prompt to *multiple models and blends answers* — which is exactly the wrong pattern for regulated data, since it would push sensitive queries to several cloud models. What you're describing is **tiered routing / local-first routing**. Keep "MOA" out of client materials; a healthcare or fund client hears that as "your data goes to multiple AI companies."

## Per-industry posture

- **Healthcare (BAA):** consider the inverted default — *everything* runs local, API is only hit when the user explicitly marks a query as general (or it hits a whitelist). Strongest posture, easiest to defend.
- **Finance (contractual LP confidentiality):** the router design is fine — self-hosting there is contractual/reputational, not a legal mandate (per the SEC Reg S-P call).

Also worth adding regardless: log every routing decision (query hash, route, model, timestamp). Auditors and LP confidentiality clauses love a paper trail.

Want me to spec this as an actual config for Ellis's deployment — router prompt, the deterministic pre-filter list, and the access-control wiring? That's the piece that makes it real.
we dont need that for Ellis
Copy — dropping the Ellis angle. The routing design stands on its own when you need it. What's it for?
for our AI CoS offering for clients
Makes sense — that's the product architecture then, not an ops detail. Let me fold it into the client-deployment skill so every private/regulated tier build gets it baked in.

The skill already has the hybrid routing *policy* — I'm adding the *implementation* layer (the 3-layer enforcement we just worked out) to that section so every Private/Regulated client build ships with it.

Done — locked into the `hermes-business-deployment` skill under Hybrid Model Routing. Every Private/Regulated client build now ships with:

- **Local router at ingress** (Qwen classifies; deterministic pre-filter first)
- **Data access control** as the real enforcement (cloud model can't touch sensitive stores, period)
- **Sanitized outbound** (no raw history to cloud)
- **Default-to-local** + healthcare inverted default + audit log
- **The naming flag** — "tiered routing," not MOA, so nobody puts "MOA" in a client deck

One thing to note: the router needs to actually get built into the deployment — right now the skill says *how* but the runtime wiring (router prompt + pre-filter list + the access-control config) is the build work. Say the word when you want me to spec that as a concrete deployable config.
question....will MOA also happen if the client wants to chat in Telegram or WhatsApp?

Yes — routing is channel-agnostic. Telegram and WhatsApp are just front doors into the same gateway; the router fires after the message lands, before model selection. Same rules apply whether it comes in via Telegram, WhatsApp, or the PWA:

- LP question over WhatsApp → stays on local Qwen
- Market research over Telegram → goes to cloud
- One routing config per client, applies to every channel they use

Only caveat: for **healthcare/PHI**, the channel itself is a separate compliance decision — the skill already says never Telegram/WhatsApp for anything touching PHI (no BAA, no E2E encryption). Routing keeps the data off the cloud model, but it doesn't make a consumer chat app HIPAA-compliant. So:

- **Finance/LP clients** → Telegram/WhatsApp fine, routing works as designed
- **Healthcare clients** → still need the compliant channel (PWA/patient portal/BAA messaging vendor) regardless of routing

Worth saying in the client deck: "same AI, same privacy rules, on whatever app you already use."
is Slack or Discord an option for Healthcare clients?

**Slack: yes. Discord: no.** Straight split:

## Slack — option, with conditions
- Slack **signs BAAs** and supports HIPAA-compliant configuration on paid plans (Business+ and up — they extended HIPAA to all paid plans in 2025). For a small practice, that's the realistic path.
- Requires setup beyond flipping a switch: signed BAA, audit logs on, message retention configured, proper user roles.
- Fits the existing architecture perfectly — department profiles already run through Slack for team access. The CoS living in the practice's Slack = internal staff comms, which is where the front desk does its work anyway.
- Best practice even with a BAA: keep raw PHI out of chat — reference the patient/portal link instead of pasting chart notes. "We don't paste PHI, and when we do it's in a BAA'd channel" is the defensible posture.

## Discord — no
- No BAA, no HIPAA posture, consumer platform with no enterprise compliance controls (no audit log guarantees, no data residency). Discord is a hard no for anything touching PHI.

## The framing for clients
- **Internal staff + CoS** (front desk, scheduling, reminders): Slack with BAA → fine. This is where the agent works.
- **Patient-facing** (appointment confirmations, intake, after-hours): still the portal or a BAA'd messaging vendor (Twilio/Sinch/Spruce) — not Slack, not consumer chat.
- **Financial/LP clients**: Slack or Discord both fine — that's contractual, not legal. (Though Slack still looks more professional.)

One honest note for the pitch: Slack holds data on Slack's cloud — the BAA covers the channel, the local router covers the model. "Your data never leaves" stays true for the AI; the channel is its own compliance story, and Slack's BAA is that story.

This is the right question to ask before we standardize — and the answer is different for the two tiers, because they use different VPS on purpose.

**Short version:** Private tier = yes, fits comfortably. Standard tier = no, a 27B model can't run on the VPS you're recommending for it.

**Why — the two tiers don't share a box:**

| | Standard tier | Private tier |
|---|---|---|
| VPS | Hostinger KVM, CPU-only, ~$7–13/mo | HOSTKEY RTX 4090 (24GB) ~$330/mo, or Vultr L40S (48GB) ~$500/mo |
| LLM | Cloud API (client's key) | Self-hosted Qwen3.8-27b via Ollama |
| Can it host 27B locally? | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |

**Private tier — plenty of room, accurate and fast:**
- Qwen3.8-27b at Q4 ≈ **17GB VRAM + ~2GB KV cache ≈ 19GB**. Fits an RTX 4090's 24GB with ~5GB headroom; L40S's 48GB leaves ~30GB.
- Hermes doesn't touch the GPU. It runs on CPU/RAM — gateway ~1.6GB, plus a few hundred MB per profile/conversation, ~3GB total. The RTX 4090 box ships with 64GB RAM, so Hermes uses ~3GB of 64GB.
- **The key fact:** Hermes eats CPU/RAM, the model eats GPU VRAM. They don't compete. On this box it's ~30–80 tok/s (3–5× reading speed) and full Q4 accuracy. This is already our documented architecture — nothing changes except the model tag.

**Standard tier — it won't run, period:**
- A $7–13/mo Hostinger KVM is CPU-only with 4–16GB RAM. Qwen3.8-27b needs ~17GB *plus* KV cache — it doesn't even fit, and even if it did, **27B on CPU runs at 1–3 tok/s** (our own notes call that "unusable for interactive chat").
- There's no way to "make it fit" by co-locating with Hermes — on a CPU box they *compete* for the same RAM, and the model loses.

**On "accurate":** co-locating Hermes with the model never reduces accuracy — that's set by the Q4 quantization (near-full) and the model itself. The only thing that kills accuracy is over-quantizing (Q2/Q3) to squeeze onto a smaller box, which you'd only be tempted to do on the Standard tier — another reason not to try it there.

**So the recommendation doesn't change:**
- **Private/Regulated** → self-host Qwen3.8-27b on the GPU box. Works, fast, accurate.
- **Standard** → keep cloud API. If you want Qwen in the standard tier, run it via API (OpenRouter), but honestly **DeepSeek V4 Flash ($0.22/$0.66) is cheaper than Qwen's API ($0.40/$3)** — so there's no cost reason to standardize standard-tier clients on Qwen either.

If you actually want "one default model everywhere," the only way to get Qwen3.8-27b on the Standard tier is to upgrade it to a GPU box — and that turns a $750/mo tier with a $7 VPS into a $330/mo infra line, wrecking the margin. Not worth it.

---
name: news-recency-verification
description: Verify news fits a rolling window via source timestamps.
---

# News Recency Verification

Use when a task requires stories/events from "the last 24 hours", a rolling-window news gate, a recency audit, or verifying *when* an event actually happened (announcements, rulings, releases, filings). The headline date is NOT the event date; aggregator dates are NOT proof.

## Core method

1. **Fetch the primary source and read machine-readable timestamps.** Run `scripts/fetch_article_meta.py <url>...` (urllib + HTMLParser, zero deps — works when `web_extract` is unavailable, e.g. a search-only `web.extract_backend`). It returns the page title, meta timestamps (`article:published_time`, schema.org `datePublished`, `date.created`, `date.available`) and cleaned article text.
2. **Normalize to UTC.** Meta timestamps are usually ISO-8601 with offsets (e.g. `2026-08-04T15:00:49+00:00`, `2026-08-05 11:25:17 +02:00`). Convert everything to UTC before comparing to your cutoff.
3. **Compare against the cutoff.** `CUTOFF_UTC = RUN_UTC - window`. Delta must be >= 0 to qualify. Save every timestamp in the audit.
4. **When the primary page lacks meta timestamps**, fetch a syndicated copy of the same official press release (BusinessWire/GlobeNewswire mirrors such as financialcontent.com carry `datePublished` in schema.org JSON-LD). Prefer the same release, not a news rewrite.
5. **Distinguish article date from underlying-event date.** Coverage published today often describes an event from days ago (e.g. an Aug 5 article about a July 31 court ruling). When coverage is fresh but the event is old, go to the official source (agency/regulator/court press pages) and find the actual announcement/ruling date before including or excluding.
6. **Write a recency audit** recording: RUN_UTC, CUTOFF_UTC, each included story's official timestamp + delta from cutoff, and each investigated-but-excluded story with its reason. Deliver the audit alongside the content.

## Pitfalls

- **Headline date ≠ event date.** A story "qualifies" only on the underlying event's timestamp. A fresh follow-up article about an older event does not reset the clock.
- **`article:modified_time` ≠ published time.** Use published/created fields for the event; modified time only confirms the page changed.
- **Timezones.** Compare UTC-normalized values. An event at 13:00:00Z fails a 13:57:10Z cutoff — being "on the same day" is not enough.
- **Search snippets are not verification.** Open the source and read the meta tags; snippets round dates to day granularity.
- **Aggregator roundup dates are the least reliable layer.** Never use them for the audit; use them only to point at primary sources.

## Worked example (Aug 5, 2026 run, cutoff 13:57:10Z)

- NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super — blog `article:published_time` `2026-08-04T15:00:49Z` → delta +1:03:39 → **included**.
- Cloudflare Wallets — blog `article:published_time` `2026-08-04T13:00:00Z` → 57 min before cutoff → **excluded** (same-day story, fails the gate).
- German court ruling vs Suno — Euronews article dated Aug 5, but GEMA/official pages showed the ruling was handed down July 31 → **excluded** despite fresh coverage.
- Anaconda press release — primary page `datePublished` `2026-08-04T14:53:12Z` → **included**.

## Deliverable shape

`recency-audit.md` next to the content pack: RUN_UTC, CUTOFF_UTC, per-included-story timestamp + delta + PASS, per-excluded-story timestamp/reason. This makes the gate auditable and lets a reviewer re-check any story in seconds.

Here's the read, Reggie.

## Short answer
Sort of — but not for the stuff that actually matters. SSD Nodes is fine for **staging/dev/PoC boxes and low-stakes self-hosted client instances**, but I would **not** put the production CoS core on it.

## What they're actually selling

| Plan | RAM | vCPU | Disk | Effective $/mo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small | 8GB | 2 | 160GB SSD | $5.50 |
| Medium | 16GB | 4 | 320GB SSD | $9.42 |
| 2X-Large | 32GB | 8 | 480GB SSD | $11.08 |
| 4X-Large | 48GB | 12 | 720GB NVMe | ~$16 |
| **8X-Large** | **64GB** | 12 | 1.2TB NVMe | **$18** |
| 16X-Large | 96GB | 12 | 1.92TB NVMe | $23 |
| Business VPS | 72GB | 12 | 1.8TB NVMe | from $99 |

Prices above are the **3-year lock-in**. Monthly billing costs more. All chips are **"Intel Silver"** (older Xeon Silver), and there's **no dedicated/managed option** — they explicitly don't sell dedicated servers. It's unmanaged.

## The real catches for our stack

1. **"Vippy" is oversubscription.** Their FAQ literally frames their low price around "optimize resource sharing." That's a noisy-neighbor setup — CPU is bursty, not guaranteed. Our CoS workloads that hurt are the CPU-bound ones: self-hosted TTS/voice cloning and any local model inference. Those will see latency spikes and get throttled right when you need them.

2. **Client data isolation.** NextCap private clients ($2K–$4.5K/mo) are paying for a self-hosted instance with their own data. Multi-tenant, oversubscribed shared VPS is the wrong isolation story for a service that sells trust and SLAs. No dedicated option = can't fix that.

3. **Memory-bound is where it shines.** Hermes + Mongo + Redis + a few Python workers that *call* cloud LLM APIs (deepseek, Kie.ai, auxiliary.vision) is mostly RAM-hungry, not CPU-hungry. On that front, the 64GB @ $18/mo is genuinely good value — hard to beat anywhere at that RAM-per-dollar.

## My call

- ✅ **Use it for:** a cheap always-on dev/staging box, a test-drive CoS instance (like the Miles test-drive), or a single non-critical client where RAM is the bottleneck and CPU jitter is tolerable.
- ❌ **Don't use it for:** NextCap private-client production, anything running self-hosted TTS/voice, or BizGrowth/AthleteEdge client-facing dashboards with uptime expectations.
- The **8X-Large (64GB/$18)** is the only plan I'd touch — that RAM is the value. Below that, the "Silver" vCPU count is too weak for an agent stack plus TTS.

We already host the important stuff on our own VPSes (`/opt/hermes-nextcap`, Emergent, Vercel). SSD Nodes doesn't beat any of those on reliability — it beats them on price only.

Want me to spin up a trial on the 8X-Large and actually benchmark our TTS + agent load on it before we commit to anything? That's the only way to know if the Vippy oversubscription bites in practice.

messages.content: can you give me the breakdown of how we will build the AI CoS for a new client? What will be the process after they sign the agreement?

Here's the full post-signature playbook, reggie. It's the turn-key onboarding flow — you do the human consultative work, i do everything else.

## The build — after they sign

**Day 0 — kickoff booked**
- Setup fee collected, interview scheduled.
- Nothing technical happens yet.

**Step 1 — you interview the founder (30–45 min)**
- Record the call. Topics: business model, daily workflow, team structure, pain points, tools, comms style, what they want automated.
- Save transcript to `~/transcripts/<client>.txt`. This is the single most important input.

**Step 2 — client sets up their own API key (5 min)**
- They create a DeepSeek/OpenAI account in *their* name, fund $20–50, hand you the key.
- They pay their own compute from day one — no margin erosion, no lock-in to our keys.
- (Or upsell Managed LLM Access at $100/mo if they don't want to touch a key.)

**Step 3 — i deploy (30 sec standard / ~10 min private)**
- **Standard tier** → provision an isolated `HERMES_HOME` on our multi-tenant VPS + a systemd gateway unit. One profile = Chief of Staff, sees everything.
- **Private/regulated tier** → dedicated GPU VPS, self-hosted Qwen 27B, no data leaves the box. Same build, different host.
- Telegram bot created (primary channel), WhatsApp optional.

**Step 4 — the agent configures *itself* (2 min)**
- I drop the transcript in. The agent turns it into:
  - `SOUL.md` — identity, voice, operating context
  - Memory seeds — business facts, people, processes, tools
  - Skill config — what to load, what to skip
  - Initial cron jobs — morning briefing, weekly digest
  - 3–5 clarifying questions for gaps

**Step 5 — the agent interviews the client (10 min, automatic)**
- First time they message the bot, it introduces itself and fills gaps conversationally.
- *"Reggie mentioned you're launching Q3…"* — asks about team, pain points, comms preferences.
- Sets up the first cron job **live during the conversation.**

**Step 6 — you tune (week 1)**
- Watch the first few days. Add skills, tweak cron, adjust voice. Then mostly hands-off.

## Why this order
- You do the high-value consultative work (the interview).
- The client watches the agent configure itself — that's the "wow" moment.
- ~30 seconds of terminal time per client, from you.

## The one decision that matters
Standard vs private/regulated changes **only step 3** (host + model). Everything else — interview, self-config, client interview, tuning — is identical. So don't let tier choice complicate the process; it's an infra switch, not a workflow change.

Want me to turn this into a one-page client-facing "what happens after you sign" doc, or a checklist we run per client? I can also wire the day-0 kickoff + step-6 tune reminders into your cron so nothing slips.
Every client will be on their OWN VPS. The VPS host will be determined by what tier Standard, Private/Regulated, Private Frontier/Regulated Frontier
not quite complete because there's nothing in here about needing to get an eSIM from Tello if the client wants to use the WhatsApp channel
Both corrections locked. Here's the fixed build process — and i'm updating the skill so it stops saying "shared VPS" for standard clients.

Skill updated. Here's the corrected build.

## Tier → VPS (every client, their own box)

| Tier | VPS host | Model |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | Dedicated CPU VPS (Hostinger KVM ~$7–13/mo) | Cloud AI — client's own API key |
| **Private/Regulated** | HOSTKEY RTX 4090 ~$330/mo — *healthcare → Vultr L40S ~$500/mo (BAA)* | Self-hosted Qwen 27B |
| **Regulated Frontier** | GPU cluster — Atlantic.Net A100 (healthcare BAA) / HOSTKEY·RunPod (financial) | Self-hosted V4-Flash |

No multi-tenant. Tier picks the box and the model — nothing else changes.

## The build — after they sign

**Day 0 — kickoff**
- Setup fee collected, interview scheduled, tier locked (tier determines the VPS).

**Step 1 — you interview the founder (30–45 min)**
- Record it. Business model, workflow, team, pain points, tools, comms style, what they want automated.
- Transcript → `~/transcripts/<client>.txt`.

**Step 2 — client API key (Standard tier only)**
- They create DeepSeek/OpenAI in *their* name, fund $20–50, hand you the key.
- Private/Frontier skip this — self-hosted, no key.

**Step 3 — provision their own VPS (host by tier above)**
- Standard: Hostinger KVM. Private: HOSTKEY RTX 4090 (or Vultr L40S if healthcare). Frontier: GPU cluster.
- Isolated `HERMES_HOME` + systemd gateway unit on that box.

**Step 3b — WhatsApp channel (optional, only if they want it)**
- Telegram is primary, always set up. WhatsApp is a separate ~30–60 min per-client task:
  1. Buy a **Tello eSIM** (~$5/mo, real US MVNO number + SMS). Not a data-only eSIM, not VoIP.
  2. Install on a phone/rig, confirm it gets SMS.
  3. `hermes whatsapp-cloud` → register the number → receive the one SMS code.
  4. Delete the eSIM profile (keep the Tello line active ~$5/mo — cancel it and the number recycles, a stranger can hijack the client's CoS).
  5. Cloudflare **named** tunnel for the webhook (stable URL).
- One eSIM slot handles every client sequentially — install, verify, delete, next.

**Step 4 — agent self-configures from transcript (2 min)**
- SOUL.md, memory seeds, skills, initial cron jobs, 3–5 clarifying questions.

**Step 5 — agent interviews the client (10 min, automatic)**
- First message = intro + fill gaps + set the first cron job live.

**Step 6 — you tune (week 1)**
- Watch the first few days, add skills, tweak voice. Then hands-off.

## Two flags to know before you promise them

- **WhatsApp 24h window:** client-initiated chat works forever, but the CoS can't *proactively* push a morning briefing unless the client messaged in the last 24h (Hermes doesn't support templates yet). Proactive stuff routes through Telegram — WhatsApp is reactive chat. So position WhatsApp as "text it anytime, it replies" not "it pushes you updates."
- **eSIM is one-time:** the number's only needed for the single verification SMS. After that Meta owns the number and the SIM is irrelevant to delivery.

Want me to fold this into a one-page client-facing "what happens next" doc, and add the Tello eSIM + VPS-provisioning steps as a reusable per-client checklist?
i'm not sure what you mean regarding proactive stuff only routes through Telegram. Can you explain? I am using both Telegram and WhatsApp and I dont really see a difference

The difference is about **who starts the conversation** — and it only matters when the bot reaches out first.

## Reactive vs proactive

- **Reactive** = client texts first, CoS replies. This works identically on both channels, forever. This is probably 100% of what you've seen — which is exactly why they look the same to you.
- **Proactive** = the CoS reaches out on its own (morning briefing, a reminder, an alert). This is where the two channels split.

## The rule

**Telegram:** the bot can message you anytime, any reason. No limits.

**WhatsApp Cloud API** (the official Meta path we use for clients): Meta has a rule that a business can only message a customer within **24 hours** of the customer's last message. Outside that window, the business can only message using a pre-approved "template" — and Hermes doesn't support templates yet. So a push outside the window just gets blocked by Meta (error 131047).

## Concrete example

Client's morning briefing fires at 6:30am.

- They texted the CoS last night → briefing lands on **both** channels. ✅
- They last texted 2 days ago → WhatsApp blocks the push ❌, Telegram delivers it ✅.

Same cron job. Different result. That's the entire difference.

## Why you don't see it

Two possible reasons, honestly:

1. You've only ever done reactive stuff on WhatsApp (texted it, got a reply) — that never hits the wall.
2. Your *own* WhatsApp bots likely run on the Baileys bridge, which has **no** 24h rule (that's the unofficial connector — no limit, but ban risk). The 24h window is specific to the Cloud API, which is what we have to use for clients because Meta won't ban an official account.

## What it means for the build

For a client who wants **both**: Telegram = the "it pushes you updates" channel (briefings, reminders, alerts). WhatsApp = the "text it anytime and it replies" channel.

For a client who wants **WhatsApp only**: they lose the proactive push until Hermes supports templates — so we flag it at sign-up and steer the recurring stuff to Telegram.

That's the whole thing. Does that clear it up?
i still dont think that true regarding whatsapp. i get morning briefs daily. i have it tied to an actual phone number like we would for each client
You're right to push on that — let me verify what you're actually running instead of arguing from the skill.

You're right, and i was wrong. I checked your actual setup instead of trusting the skill.

## What you're actually running

Your WhatsApp is on the **Baileys** connector — not the Cloud API. I confirmed it:

- `/opt/hermes-nextcap/whatsapp` and `bizgrowth-cos/platforms/whatsapp` — Baileys session dirs, with `WHATSAPP_MODE`, `WHATSAPP_GROUP_POLICY`, `WHATSAPP_ALLOW_ALL_USERS` set.
- Zero `WHATSAPP_CLOUD_*` variables anywhere.

Baileys has **no 24-hour window.** That's exactly why your morning briefs push daily. You're 100% correct.

## The mistake i made

I was describing the **Cloud API** (`hermes whatsapp-cloud` — the official Meta path), which *does* have the 24h rule. That's a different connector you're not running. I told you a limitation of a system you don't use, and presented it as if it applied to WhatsApp generally. My bad.

| | Baileys (what you run) | Cloud API (what i was describing) |
|---|---|---|
| Official Meta? | No — ban risk | Yes |
| Proactive pushes (morning brief) | ✅ works | ❌ blocked after 24h |
| Groups | Full | DMs only |
| Real number needed | Yes (like yours) | Yes |

## What it actually means for clients

If we deploy clients the **same way you run it** — Baileys + one real number each — then WhatsApp does proactive fine. No difference between the channels, no "Telegram-only" routing. Your instinct was right.

The skill locked "Cloud API for clients" purely to avoid ban risk, but that trade actually sacrifices the morning briefing (the flagship feature) to dodge a risk your own long-running Baileys setup hasn't hit.

## My recommendation

Flip the client default to **Baileys + one real number per client** (your setup). Keep the Tello eSIM step — Baileys still needs a real number per client to pair. Offer Cloud API only as an opt-in for a client who specifically wants the "official, can't-get-banned" path and accepts losing proactive pushes.

The one caveat i'll still flag: Baileys is unofficial, so the number has *some* ban exposure. Using a real carrier number (Tello) and low-volume 1:1 chat keeps that risk low — which is exactly your current setup and it's been fine.

Want me to flip the skill so the client default is Baileys instead of Cloud API?
Are you telling me that the Hermes Agent way to connect to Telegram as a channel is NOT an "official" way to connect?

No — Telegram is a completely different situation. Let me be precise, because i was sloppy with the word "official."

## Telegram: one official way, no catch

When Hermes connects to Telegram, it uses your **BotFather token** — which *is* Telegram's official Bot API. That's the first-party, supported, intended way to use Telegram. Telegram built the Bot API specifically so people could build bots this way. Nothing unofficial about it, no ban risk, no 24-hour window, no eSIM needed.

That's exactly why Telegram is the primary channel — it's clean on every axis.

## WhatsApp: the split is *inside* WhatsApp, not Hermes

The "official vs unofficial" thing is a **WhatsApp-specific** problem, because Meta doesn't offer the same open bot API Telegram does. Meta gives you two routes:

| Route | What it is | Official? | Proactive pushes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cloud API** | Meta's own business API | ✅ official | ❌ 24h rule |
| **Baileys** | Third-party reverse-engineer of WhatsApp's internal protocol | ❌ unofficial | ✅ works |

So when i said "unofficial," i was talking about the **Baileys connector for WhatsApp** — not Telegram, and not Hermes itself.

## The honest summary

- **Telegram** = official, no caveats. Always the default.
- **WhatsApp Cloud API** = official, but the 24h rule guts proactive.
- **WhatsApp Baileys** (what you run) = unofficial, but full features — the tradeoff is Meta *can* ban the number, since it's not their supported path.

So my earlier correction still stands, but the word choice was misleading: i made it sound like "unofficial" applied to how Hermes connects in general. It doesn't. It's strictly a WhatsApp-Baileys thing.

Does that line it up?
Sorry....i meant WhatsAPpp

Right — yes, exactly. That's the whole point.

The way Hermes connects **you** to WhatsApp right now (Baileys, the `hermes whatsapp` path) is **not** Meta's official API. It's a third-party reverse-engineer of WhatsApp's internal protocol. That's what i meant by "unofficial."

Hermes also has a second, *official* WhatsApp connector — `hermes whatsapp-cloud`, which uses Meta's real Cloud API. Two different connectors, two different variable sets:

| Connector | Meta official? | Proactive (morning brief) | Ban risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hermes whatsapp` (Baileys) — **what you run** | ❌ no | ✅ works | ⚠️ yes, Meta can ban it |
| `hermes whatsapp-cloud` (Cloud API) | ✅ yes | ❌ 24h rule | ✅ none |

So:

- You're currently on the **unofficial** one → that's why daily briefs work, and also why there's some ban exposure.
- The **official** one is safe from bans but loses proactive pushes.

That's the full picture. Your call on which way clients go — i'd default to Baileys (what you run) since the flagship feature depends on it, but the tradeoff is real.

messages.content: Based on the information you know about our Biz Growth AI Chief of Staff offering, what kind of white label pricing should I consider? I've got a potential partner that wants to white label our AI Chief of Staff offering.
Let me pull the relevant BizGrowth skills so I answer off the real offering numbers, not memory alone.
Pulled the two BizGrowth skills and the deployment playbook. I've got the real numbers — one more look at the margin framework so my wholesale math is grounded, not guessed.

Here's the straight answer, grounded in your actual numbers.

## First — white label ≠ your commission model

Your consultant/referral program (25% / 15% / 10%) is for partners who bring you clients *you* bill and brand. White label is the inverse: **the partner owns the relationship, sells under their brand, and pays you a wholesale rate.** You're invisible. That changes the math and the risks, so don't reach for the commission table here.

## Recommended wholesale pricing

Your real marginal cost per standard seat is ~$60/mo (shared VPS + client's own API key). Regulated is ~$330/mo (GPU). So you've got huge room to give the partner a margin and still win.

| Tier | Your retail | Wholesale to partner | Partner sells at | Your margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard CoS | $2,000 + $750/mo | $1,500 + **$450/mo** | $750+ (their call) | ~$390/mo (~87%) |
| Regulated (Qwen) | $3,000 + $2,000/mo | $2,500 + **$1,400/mo** | $2,000+ | ~$1,070/mo |
| Regulated Frontier | $3,000 + $4,500/mo | $3,000 + **$3,000/mo** | $4,500+ | ~$2,670/mo |

**Rule of thumb: wholesale ≈ 60–65% of retail monthly, setup at 75–100%.** Setup stays near-full because it's your actual deployment labor — there's no reason to hand the partner margin on your sweat.

## Terms that protect you (non-negotiable)

- **Minimum volume floor** — e.g. $2,500/mo wholesale or 5 seats within 90 days. White label only pays off if they actually bring volume.
- **Setup is not discountable** — labor is labor.
- **12-month term per seat**, no month-to-month white-label seats.
- **Support split in writing** — if the partner handles first-line support, they earn the bigger spread. If *you're* their anonymous tech team, that support labor gets priced in (add $100–200/mo wholesale or a support retainer).
- **Non-solicitation both ways** — partner can't poach your playbook/skills and cut you out; you don't touch their clients.

## The real tradeoff you need to stare at

White label means you **give up the relationship, the retention moat, and the strategy-session/upsell revenue** on every one of those clients. That's why the wholesale price has to hold your ~85% margin — if you price it like a referral (10%), you're subsidizing someone else's brand.

Before you quote this partner a number, nail two things:

1. **True white label vs "powered by BizGrowth"** — full white label (you vanish) should cost them more wholesale than a co-brand where you keep a small logo/line.
2. **Who does support** — this alone swings the wholesale rate $100–200/mo.

If you tell me which of those two it is, I'll lock a final number. Otherwise, quote them the $450/$1,400/$3,000 wholesale table with the floor and 12-month term attached.

messages.content: i have a question about our AI CoS for medical practices. If we install on a VPS, install their own LLM, do we need a BAA?

Short answer: yes, you still need a BAA — self-hosting the LLM removes one, but it doesn't remove the main one.

Here's how it breaks down, Phil's take:

**The BAA you can't skip**
- A medical practice is a HIPAA "covered entity." If your CoS touches PHI (patient names, appointments, intake, billing — basically anything a medical CoS does), then *your company* becomes their "business associate."
- That means you sign a BAA *with the practice.* Period. Self-hosting or VPS doesn't change this — it's about whether you're handling their patient data, not where the servers live.

**What self-hosting the LLM actually buys you**
- This is the real upside: run an open model (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) on your own box and the PHI never leaves your environment. So you need **no BAA with the model vendor** — Meta/Mistral never see the data.
- Compare: use OpenAI/Anthropic/GPT-4o APIs and now *you* need a BAA with them, plus zero-data-retention turned on. Self-host = that whole layer goes away.

**The VPS is the one people forget**
- If PHI sits on that VPS, the hosting provider is your *subcontractor* business associate. You need a BAA with them too.
- AWS, Azure, and GCP offer HIPAA BAAs out of the box. A random cheap VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, etc.) generally won't sign one — which quietly rules them out for PHI.

**The only scenario where you need no BAA at all**
- If the CoS never touches PHI — purely admin, no patient data. Unlikely for medical practices, but worth defining before you build. If it's truly no-PHI, HIPAA doesn't apply and the whole question evaporates.

**My rec for the offer**
1. You sign the BAA with the practice (you're the BA).
2. Host on AWS/Azure/GCP so the VPS BAA is covered.
3. Self-host the LLM to kill the AI-vendor BAA and keep data in-house.
4. Bake in encryption at rest + in transit, access controls, and audit logs — a BAA obligates the Security Rule whether the practice asks or not.

One caveat, and I'm not going to soften it: I'm not your lawyer, and the exact answer hinges on who actually controls that VPS (yours vs. theirs) and whether the CoS touches PHI at all. If you're about to pitch this as "HIPAA compliant," have counsel give it one pass first — it's a $500 review against a much bigger liability.

Done digging. Here's the real answer — and it's better than what we left on last night, because Hermes already has the machinery to do this natively. You don't build a custom routing layer.

## The key fact we didn't have last night

Hermes's gateway has a **profile multiplexer** (`gateway.multiplex_profiles`). One gateway process fronts **many client profiles**, and it routes each incoming chat to the right profile by who's messaging. This is *exactly* the "one number serves all clients, route by sender" model I described — but it's built in, same as Telegram chat IDs. Bonus: it also fixes the PII isolation gap the command center flagged (each client profile has its own memory).

So the architecture is:

```
ONE WhatsApp number (Cloud API)
        │
   default gateway  (multiplex_profiles: on + allowlist)
        │  routes sender → profile
        ▼
 client-1 profile · client-2 profile · client-3 profile …
   (own memory, own skills, own home channel)
```

## How to connect a NEW client (the part you asked about)

- **One-time Meta setup:** one Meta Business account, one app, one WABA, one phone number, a permanent System User token. `hermes whatsapp-cloud` is a wizard that walks you through it.
- **Per new client (30 seconds):** create their named profile (you already do this), set their `WHATSAPP_CLOUD_HOME_CHANNEL` = their phone number, add them to the allowlist. Done. They text the one number, the multiplexer hands the thread to *their* CoS.

## The two real constraints to know before you commit

1. **The phone number.** Cloud API needs one *real* business number that can receive a verification SMS/call. Meta rejects VoIP (that's why Google Voice was the wrong instinct). Get one dedicated prepaid SIM ($5–15, keep it active with a call every 90 days), register it to WhatsApp Business, and the SIM lives in a drawer after. One number, not one per client.

2. **The 24-hour window (the actual gotcha).** Cloud API only lets you send *unsolicited* messages within 24h of the client's last message — outside that you need a pre-approved Meta template, and Hermes **doesn't support templates yet**. Reactive chat (client texts → CoS replies) works forever. What breaks: proactively pushing the morning briefing/reminders to a client who hasn't messaged in a day.

## My recommendation

- **Use Cloud API, not the Baileys bridge.** Baileys has no 24h limit, but it's unofficial and ban-prone — a client's CoS number getting banned mid-relationship is worse than the template gap. Cloud API is the official, ban-proof path.
- **One number to start**, WhatsApp as the *secondary* channel (Telegram stays primary). Route proactive briefings through Telegram; for WhatsApp clients, the message-first pattern works until Hermes ships templates.

Yeah, you can — but first let me clear up the terminology, because "account" is doing three different jobs here and that's the source of the confusion.

## The three "accounts" in WhatsApp

| Thing | What it is | How many you need |
|---|---|---|
| **WhatsApp Business Account (WABA)** | A *container* that holds phone numbers. Not a phone app. Lives inside your Meta Business account. | 1 (or a few) |
| **Phone number** | The actual identity clients see ("BizGrowth AI"). Each has its own display name. | **1 per brand**, not per client |
| **Meta Business account** (Business Manager) | Your company's top-level Meta login. Holds apps + WABAs. | 1 |

The important rule: **one phone number lives in exactly one WABA**, and one number has **one display name**. But one WABA can hold **a couple dozen numbers** (more on request), and your one Meta Business account can hold **multiple WABAs**.

## So "different businesses" maps like this

```

## Why this matters for your CoS

The one constraint that could trip you: a single number can only present **one** name. So if a NextCap client and a BizGrowth client both text the *same* number, they both see the same sender name. If you're white-labeling the CoS under one brand ("Miles" / BizGrowth AI) — which you are — one number is all you need, and every client just sees your CoS brand. Perfect.

If you later want Active Recovery to *look* like Active Recovery and not BizGrowth, that's one more number (same WABA), not a new account or a new build.

## My read for you

Start with **one WABA, one number** branded as your CoS offering. Don't spin up a number per brand until a brand actually demands its own face. The whole point of the multiplexer is that the *brand* is the identity boundary, and *clients* are just routed beneath it.

## The catch: "own number" ≠ "own name"

A WhatsApp number's **display name** goes through Meta approval and has to match a **real business you're authorized to represent**. So:

- If every client's CoS shows **"BizGrowth AI"** (your brand) → no problem, but then per-client numbers give you *no branding benefit*, only isolation.
- If you want each client to see **their own company name** → Meta will ask you to prove you're authorized to represent "Acme Industries" before approving that name. That's a letter-of-authorization dance per client.

So the white-label dream (client sees *their* number, *their* name) is real but has per-client friction. Isolation is the easy part.

## Real per-client overhead

- One number per client = source it, register it, verify via SMS, get a display name approved (~24–48h each) — **every single onboarding**.

- One more number+token to track per client in ops.

## My recommendation: split it by tier

| Tier | WhatsApp setup | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Regulated / Enterprise** ($2K+/mo) | **Dedicated number per client** | Isolation + "your own CoS number" is a selling point, and $2K/mo buys the provisioning. |
| **Standard** ($750/mo) | **One shared number + multiplexer** | Scales to unlimited clients, 30-second onboarding, full isolation already. |

The architecture runs **both at once** — the multiplexer fronts the shared number for standard clients, and each regulated client gets a dedicated number bound to their own profile. That's the setup that matches how you actually sell.

**A)** Per-client numbers for *everyone* — full white-label, but every $750 client now carries a number-provisioning + name-approval overhead.

**B)** Tier-split (my call) — dedicated numbers for regulated/enterprise, shared+multiplex for standard.

## The trap: most web eSIMs are data-only

The travel-style eSIM providers (Airalo, Holafly, Nomad, etc.) sell **data-only** eSIMs — **no phone number, no SMS**. WhatsApp verification needs a real number that can receive one SMS code, so those are useless here. That's the wrong product.

## What "web-based eSIM" actually means for you

You don't need a *travel* eSIM. You need a **real US carrier number, activated online** — and the MVNOs do exactly that: eSIM, instant online activation, real number + SMS, no store visit.

| Provider | Plan | Why it fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Tello** (my default) | ~$5/mo | eSIM, online-only, real number, SMS. Cheapest keep-alive. |
| **US Mobile** | ~$8-10/mo | eSIM, online, real number + SMS. |
| Mint Mobile | $15/mo (3-mo min) | Fine, but overkill for a verification number. |

eSIM vs physical SIM makes **zero difference to Meta** — it just needs a real (non-VoIP) carrier number that can receive one SMS.

## The one rule that matters

You only need the number **live long enough to receive one verification code**. After that, Meta owns the number and the SIM/eSIM can sit in a drawer. **But** — keep a minimal plan active ($5/mo) so the carrier never recycles the number out from under a client, because a recycled number can be re-registered by a stranger and hijack that client's CoS.

## Avoid the gray-market path

The "WhatsApp virtual number" / temp-number / SMS-activation resellers sell **recycled numbers**. For a personal test account, whatever — for a *client's production CoS*, a recycled number getting claimed by someone else is a client-ending event. Don't.

1. Buy a Tello eSIM number (~$5).
2. Activate online, confirm it receives SMS.
3. Run `hermes whatsapp-cloud` → register the number to your WABA → receive the one SMS code.
4. Set the number's display name (your CoS brand, or the client's with a letter-of-authorization if you want full white-label).
5. Bind it to that client's profile. Done.

Cost per client: ~$5 one-time + ~$5/mo keep-alive.

Here's the mechanics:

- **The number lives with the carrier, not your phone.** When you "delete" an eSIM profile from your phone, the Tello line stays active on your account (you keep paying ~$5/mo). Deleting the eSIM just removes your phone's access to it — it does *not* cancel the number.
- **So the flow is:** install client-1's eSIM → receive the SMS code → verify WhatsApp → delete that eSIM → install client-2's eSIM → repeat. One eSIM slot handles every client sequentially.
- **After all clients are set up, remove every eSIM from your phone.** The bots run on the server (Hermes gateway), totally independent of your device. Your phone was never more than a temporary SMS receiver.

Two things that make this cleaner:

1. **You can keep your own line the whole time.** Most phones run dual eSIM — your personal number stays active in one slot while you add/remove client eSIMs in the other.
2. **A spare/old phone as a dedicated "verification rig"** is the low-friction version — install each eSIM there, verify, remove. Never touches your daily phone.

It runs today at no cost, but it's the little sibling — 14B and a generation back — so it'll undersell the 27B on reasoning. Wired up and verified. Here's the full picture:

**✅ Working.** `groq-qwen` → `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` is live with your key. Real test calls came back clean. The answer quality is genuinely good — here's the model on a fund question:

> *"A capital call is a request from a fund manager for a limited partner to contribute committed cash into the fund, whereas a distribution is a payment from the fund back to the limited partner returning invested capital and/or profits."*

Accurate, plain-English, no fluff. It handles the CoS workload fine.

**⚠️ One real finding you need to know:** Groq serves Qwen3.6-27B in **thinking mode, and you can't turn it off** — I tried `enable_thinking:false` and Groq rejects it. So every answer silently burns ~400-500 tokens of internal reasoning before it replies (that capital-call answer: 29 prompt tokens → 435 completion tokens for a 45-word sentence — ~10× overhead). Slower and token-heavy.

**This is NOT what we'd ship.** The self-hosted Ollama `qwen3.6:27b` is the **non-thinking instruct build** — it answers directly, no reasoning preamble. So the Groq test is a good *quality* check, but a poor proxy for *feel and latency*. Treat the Groq output as "the model's brain, with the verbosity dial stuck on."

**To talk to it yourself, switch the model in this chat:**

```
/model groq-qwen
```

or set it as default with `hermes model groq-qwen`. Then your next messages route to Qwen instead of DeepSeek — ask it to draft an LP email, research a deal, whatever, and it'll respond as the model.

One more note while I had the model list open: Groq also exposes `openai/gpt-oss-120b` — the GPT-OSS we dropped. Confirms it's real, but it scored below Qwen on reasoning, so we were right to kill it.

Want me to leave you on DeepSeek (me), or would you rather I switch the default now so you can start hammering Qwen with real CoS prompts?
are u saying that the qwen we'd ship has NO reasoning at all?

No — and that's my sloppy wording, so let me untangle the two things I accidentally collapsed:

**"Thinking mode" ≠ "reasoning ability."** They're different:

- **Reasoning** is the model's underlying ability to work through a problem. Every LLM does this internally on every answer — it's the whole point of the model.
- **Thinking mode** is just whether the model *prints out* that reasoning as a visible step-by-step trace (the `` block you saw) before giving the final answer.

Same weights, same brain either way. The only difference is whether it shows its work.

So what we'd ship (Ollama `qwen3.6:27b`, non-thinking) **absolutely reasons** — it just answers directly, without spending ~400 tokens writing out its internal monologue first. It's the same model you just saw answer the capital-call question correctly; it just skips the preamble.

**The actual tradeoff, stated honestly:**

| | Non-thinking (what we ship) | Thinking mode (what Groq gave you) |
|---|---|---|
| Reasons? | Yes, internally | Yes, out loud |
| Speed | Fast, direct | Slower |
| Token cost | Cheap | ~10× more per answer |
| Best for | Ops, drafting, scheduling — the $2K tier's bread and butter | *Hard* analytical problems, where forcing step-by-step deliberation improves accuracy |

And that last row is the real nuance: for genuinely tough problems ("model this deal's downside"), thinking mode isn't just verbosity — it often produces a *better* answer, because writing out the steps forces more compute on the problem. That's why the Frontier tier (V4-Flash) exists — for clients whose work needs that deliberation. But for the $2K operational tier, non-thinking is the right default, not a downgrade.

One correction to my own claim while we're here: I said "thinking can't be turned off on Groq." That's true of Groq's API — but the toggle exists in the model itself. On Ollama you can flip it per-task (Qwen supports a `thinking` on/off). So we'd ship non-thinking as default, and for a Private-tier client who occasionally needs deeper analysis, we can turn it on for that one task rather than buying them Frontier. That's actually a nice lever for the $2K tier I hadn't spelled out.

Net: **the Qwen we ship reasons fine — it just doesn't narrate it.** My "no reasoning" phrasing was wrong.
ok. so...what version should i use...Groq or Ollama?

**Groq — right now.** It's already wired, free, and the answer quality is the same brain you'd ship. For a "is Qwen 27B smart enough for the CoS tier" test, that's all you need.

---
name: news-recency-verification
description: Verify news fits a rolling window via source timestamps.
---

# News Recency Verification

Use when a task requires stories/events from "the last 24 hours", a rolling-window news gate, a recency audit, or verifying *when* an event actually happened (announcements, rulings, releases, filings). The headline date is NOT the event date; aggregator dates are NOT proof.

## Core method

1. **Fetch the primary source and read machine-readable timestamps.** Run `scripts/fetch_article_meta.py <url>...` (urllib + HTMLParser, zero deps — works when `web_extract` is unavailable, e.g. a search-only `web.extract_backend`). It returns the page title, meta timestamps (`article:published_time`, schema.org `datePublished`, `date.created`, `date.available`) and cleaned article text.
2. **Normalize to UTC.** Meta timestamps are usually ISO-8601 with offsets (e.g. `2026-08-04T15:00:49+00:00`, `2026-08-05 11:25:17 +02:00`). Convert everything to UTC before comparing to your cutoff.
3. **Compare against the cutoff.** `CUTOFF_UTC = RUN_UTC - window`. Delta must be >= 0 to qualify. Save every timestamp in the audit.
4. **When the primary page lacks meta timestamps**, fetch a syndicated copy of the same official press release (BusinessWire/GlobeNewswire mirrors such as financialcontent.com carry `datePublished` in schema.org JSON-LD). Prefer the same release, not a news rewrite.
5. **Distinguish article date from underlying-event date.** Coverage published today often describes an event from days ago (e.g. an Aug 5 article about a July 31 court ruling). When coverage is fresh but the event is old, go to the official source (agency/regulator/court press pages) and find the actual announcement/ruling date before including or excluding.
6. **Write a recency audit** recording: RUN_UTC, CUTOFF_UTC, each included story's official timestamp + delta from cutoff, and each investigated-but-excluded story with its reason. Deliver the audit alongside the content.

## Pitfalls

- **Headline date ≠ event date.** A story "qualifies" only on the underlying event's timestamp. A fresh follow-up article about an older event does not reset the clock.
- **`article:modified_time` ≠ published time.** Use published/created fields for the event; modified time only confirms the page changed.
- **Timezones.** Compare UTC-normalized values. An event at 13:00:00Z fails a 13:57:10Z cutoff — being "on the same day" is not enough.
- **Search snippets are not verification.** Open the source and read the meta tags; snippets round dates to day granularity.
- **Aggregator roundup dates are the least reliable layer.** Never use them for the audit; use them only to point at primary sources.

## Worked example (Aug 5, 2026 run, cutoff 13:57:10Z)

- NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super — blog `article:published_time` `2026-08-04T15:00:49Z` → delta +1:03:39 → **included**.
- Cloudflare Wallets — blog `article:published_time` `2026-08-04T13:00:00Z` → 57 min before cutoff → **excluded** (same-day story, fails the gate).
- German court ruling vs Suno — Euronews article dated Aug 5, but GEMA/official pages showed the ruling was handed down July 31 → **excluded** despite fresh coverage.
- Anaconda press release — primary page `datePublished` `2026-08-04T14:53:12Z` → **included**.

## Deliverable shape

`recency-audit.md` next to the content pack: RUN_UTC, CUTOFF_UTC, per-included-story timestamp + delta + PASS, per-excluded-story timestamp/reason. This makes the gate auditable and lets a reviewer re-check any story in seconds.

The user has provided the following instruction alongside the skill invocation: [IMPORTANT: You are running as a scheduled cron job. DELIVERY: Your final response will be automatically delivered to the user — do NOT use send_message or try to deliver the output yourself. Just produce your report/output as your final response and the system handles the rest. SILENT: If there is genuinely nothing new to report, respond with exactly "[SILENT]" (nothing else) to suppress delivery. Never combine [SILENT] with content — either report your findings normally, or say [SILENT] and nothing more.]

Research and deliver a daily briefing of the latest AI + dental industry news. Audience: a dental insurance company's senior brand & product marketing leader (Delta Dental of Arizona) — prioritize stories relevant to dental insurance, practice operations, patient experience, AI imaging/diagnostics, and marketing.

Each run:
1. Search for AI news in the dental industry from roughly the last 48 hours. Rotate search terms such as: "AI dentistry", "AI dental", "artificial intelligence dental", "dental AI startup", "AI dental insurance", "dental technology AI", "AI caries detection", "teledentistry AI". Also check dental-trade sources: Becker's Dental Review, Dental Products Report, Dentistry Today, DrBicuspid, Dental Economics, ADA News, DentistryIQ.
2. Verify recency with the `news-recency-verification` skill (read source publish timestamps — not aggregator dates). Skip anything older than ~48h unless it is clearly the most recent significant item on that topic.
3. Pick the top 3-4 most relevant stories and write each as a one-line "headline + why it matters" summary, followed by the full URL.

Format the final message exactly like this (no emojis, no hashtags, casual and brief):

**AI in Dental — <Month Day>**
- <Headline>: one line on why it matters to a dental insurer/marketer. 
  <full URL>
- (repeat for each story)

Always put each story's full URL on its own line so it is easy to copy. If nothing qualifies in the 48-hour window, say so in one line and surface the 2-3 most recent items anyway with their publish dates clearly labeled — do not force stale stories as "today's news."

**AI in Dental — August 26**

- Dental schools are using AI avatars ("John and Judy") to train students on real patient conversations: an early sign of an AI-native dentist workforce and a patient-experience play worth watching.

[IMPORTANT: The user has invoked the "linkedin-ai-news-roundup" skill, indicating they want you to follow its instructions. The full skill content is loaded below.]

---
name: linkedin-ai-news-roundup
description: Generate a casual, no-emoji LinkedIn post from the last ~24h of AI news (verified links + "what it means for us"), and publish it to the user's personal LinkedIn profile via browser automation on the user's OWN machine (with a mandatory human-confirm-before-Post pause). Research+write half runs anywhere, including on a daily cron; publish half requires the user's logged-in browser reachable by computer_use.
---

# LinkedIn AI News Roundup

Use when the user asks to "post AI news to LinkedIn", "share the latest AI news on LinkedIn", a daily AI-news LinkedIn update, or anything similar.

Two halves:
1. **Research + Write** — fully automatable, runs anywhere (including a scheduled cron). Gathers the last ~24h of AI news, verifies against primary sources, writes a casual no-emoji post.
2. **Publish** — ONLYvia browser automation against the user's OWN logged-in LinkedIn session (the desktop `computer_use` path). Never from the remote Hermes server, which has no user session and would trip bot detection / need credentials. Always pause for human confirmation before the final "Post" click.

Load `social-media-creative-production` alongside this skill for voice/caption rules — its "Voice & News-Roundup Posts" section is authoritative for tone (casual, no jargon, always include "what it means for us", open question to drive comments). Load `hermes-browser-automation` for the in-app `browser_*` tool caveats when using the server browser instead.

## Voice rules (apply every time)
- Casual, non-technical, human-to-friend tone. No jargon dumps.
- **No emojis** in the final post (user explicitly requested this).
- Always lead with the takeaway, then the stories, then an open question to drive comments.
- Include a "what it means for us" angle after each headline (1-2 sentences).
- Two-pass format is welcome: offer a short punchy version + a longer casual version.
- **Verification honesty:** flag any item sourced only from aggregator roundups as "confirm via source first" before publishing. Never present aggregator claims as confirmed fact.

## Part 1 — Research + Write (automatable, runs anywhere)

### Sources to query (fresh each run)
Use `web_search` for discovery and `web_extract` (or the source article) for verification. Prefer primary sources (vendor blogs, TechCrunch, Guardian, Ars Technica, NYT, Reuters) over aggregator roundups.

Good recurring queries:
- `AI news today <today's date>`
- `OpenAI OR Anthropic OR Google OR Meta AI announcement <date>`
- `AI agent autonomous security <recent>`
- `AI model release tracker <date>`

Filter to the **last 24 hours**. If a strong story is ~48h old but is the week's biggest item (e.g. a major model release), include it but label the recency honestly in your verbal summary to the user — NOT by faking the date in the post.

### Post structure
```
<casual hook — 1-2 sentences, the takeaway>

<3 numbered stories, each: 1-line plain-English what happened + "what it means for us" + source links>

<short "what this means for the rest of us" bullet list — 2-4 bullets>

<big-picture 1-2 sentences>

<open question to drive comments>

#hashtags (6-8, no emoji)
```

### Deliverable for draft-only / cron mode
Write the post to a file at `$HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` AND print it in chat. State clearly which items are verified vs flagged-unverified.

## Part 2 — Publish (user's own machine only, human-in-the-loop)

This half runs ONLY when the user is on a machine where Hermes's `computer_use` driver can reach a browser already logged into LinkedIn. From a remote/headless server it cannot work — say so and fall back to draft-only.

### Preconditions to confirm with the user
- "Are you logged into LinkedIn in a browser Hermes can reach on this machine?" If no, stop and deliver the draft for manual paste.
- Never ask for or type LinkedIn credentials. Never attempt `browser_navigate` to a LinkedIn login and fill a password.
- LinkedIn actively fights automation/bot logins. Pre-authentication (user already signed in) is mandatory; bot-detection may still challenge, and the user must handle any 2FA/CAPTCHA.

### Publish flow (computer_use)
1. `computer_use(action="capture", app="<browser>")` — get a screenshot + AX tree. Prefer limiting to the browser app.
2. Navigate to the LinkedIn feed / start-post composer. If not logged in (login wall visible), STOP — do not proceed; deliver draft for manual paste.
3. Open the "Start a post" composer.
4. Type the full post text into the composer textbox (`action="type"`).
5. Verify the text rendered correctly (re-capture, read the composer content).
6. **MANDATORY PAUSE:** do NOT click the final "Post" button. Tell the user the post is composed and waiting, and ask them to review + click Post themselves (or explicitly authorize Hermes to click it). This protects against accidental posts and bot flags.
7. Only after explicit user confirmation may `computer_use` click the Post button — and even then, prefer the user does it.

### Why a human-confirm pause is non-negotiable
- LinkedIn ToS gray/prohibited zone for automated profile posting; silent auto-Post risks account flags/locks.
- Prevents posting a draft with unverified items or a typo.
- The user owns the account; the agent owns the draft.

## Cron wiring (daily automated draft)
Set a daily cron that loads THIS skill + the research half only, delivers the draft to chat. Example prompt for the cron:
"Load skill linkedin-ai-news-roundup. Run Part 1 (research + write) for the last 24h of AI news. Save the post to $HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<today>.md and print it in chat. Do NOT publish — draft only. Casual voice, no emojis, include what-it-means-for-us and source links. Flag any unverified aggregator-sourced items."

Publishing stays a deliberate, user-initiated action (Part 2) on the user's machine.

## Common pitfalls
- Using emojis (user said no).
- Presenting aggregator roundups as verified fact — flag them.
- Trying to publish from the remote server browser (no session, bot-detection, credential risk) — fall back to draft.
- Typing the user's LinkedIn password — never.
- Clicking "Post" without explicit user confirmation.
- Faking a story's date to make it look <24h — be honest about recency in the chat summary.
