name: news-recency-verification
description: Verify news fits a rolling window via source timestamps.
---

# News Recency Verification

Use when a task requires stories/events from "the last 24 hours", a rolling-window news gate, a recency audit, or verifying *when* an event actually happened (announcements, rulings, releases, filings). The headline date is NOT the event date; aggregator dates are NOT proof.

## Core method

1. **Fetch the primary source and read machine-readable timestamps.** Run `scripts/fetch_article_meta.py <url>...` (urllib + HTMLParser, zero deps — works when `web_extract` is unavailable, e.g. a search-only `web.extract_backend`). It returns the page title, meta timestamps (`article:published_time`, schema.org `datePublished`, `date.created`, `date.available`) and cleaned article text.
2. **Normalize to UTC.** Meta timestamps are usually ISO-8601 with offsets (e.g. `2026-08-04T15:00:49+00:00`, `2026-08-05 11:25:17 +02:00`). Convert everything to UTC before comparing to your cutoff.
3. **Compare against the cutoff.** `CUTOFF_UTC = RUN_UTC - window`. Delta must be >= 0 to qualify. Save every timestamp in the audit.
4. **When the primary page lacks meta timestamps**, fetch a syndicated copy of the same official press release (BusinessWire/GlobeNewswire mirrors such as financialcontent.com carry `datePublished` in schema.org JSON-LD). Prefer the same release, not a news rewrite.
5. **Distinguish article date from underlying-event date.** Coverage published today often describes an event from days ago (e.g. an Aug 5 article about a July 31 court ruling). When coverage is fresh but the event is old, go to the official source (agency/regulator/court press pages) and find the actual announcement/ruling date before including or excluding.
6. **Write a recency audit** recording: RUN_UTC, CUTOFF_UTC, each included story's official timestamp + delta from cutoff, and each investigated-but-excluded story with its reason. Deliver the audit alongside the content.

## Pitfalls

- **Headline date ≠ event date.** A story "qualifies" only on the underlying event's timestamp. A fresh follow-up article about an older event does not reset the clock.
- **`article:modified_time` ≠ published time.** Use published/created fields for the event; modified time only confirms the page changed.
- **Timezones.** Compare UTC-normalized values. An event at 13:00:00Z fails a 13:57:10Z cutoff — being "on the same day" is not enough.
- **Search snippets are not verification.** Open the source and read the meta tags; snippets round dates to day granularity.
- **Aggregator roundup dates are the least reliable layer.** Never use them for the audit; use them only to point at primary sources.

## Worked example (Aug 5, 2026 run, cutoff 13:57:10Z)

- NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super — blog `article:published_time` `2026-08-04T15:00:49Z` → delta +1:03:39 → **included**.
- Cloudflare Wallets — blog `article:published_time` `2026-08-04T13:00:00Z` → 57 min before cutoff → **excluded** (same-day story, fails the gate).
- German court ruling vs Suno — Euronews article dated Aug 5, but GEMA/official pages showed the ruling was handed down July 31 → **excluded** despite fresh coverage.
- Anaconda press release — primary page `datePublished` `2026-08-04T14:53:12Z` → **included**.

## Deliverable shape

`recency-audit.md` next to the content pack: RUN_UTC, CUTOFF_UTC, per-included-story timestamp + delta + PASS, per-excluded-story timestamp/reason. This makes the gate auditable and lets a reviewer re-check any story in seconds.

## LinkedIn — LONG version (also saved to linkedin-post-long.md)

Three things moved in AI in the last 24 hours, and all three are the kind of news that quietly changes what you'll pay for AI and who's selling it to you. No hype, just what happened and what it means for a small business.

**1. SpaceX closed its $60B deal for Cursor.** Cursor is the AI coding tool that developers use to write software faster — you may never type code yourself and still feel this one, because the software your business runs on gets built with tools like it. Elon Musk's SpaceX just finished buying it in a deal worth $60 billion. Cursor's announcement says the company now has access to "the largest fleet of GPUs in the world." What it means for us: the AI coding market is consolidating into the same companies that own the chips and the cloud. When the tool maker and the compute provider are one company, expect bundles, pricing moves, and a lot more vertical integration. That can mean better products — and it can also mean less choice.

**2. Bloomberg: $70B in hidden credit backstops are propping up the AI buildout.** Bond investors are worried about roughly $70 billion in "phantom liabilities" — residual-value guarantees that don't show up on AI companies' balance sheets. Nvidia is preparing to backstop debt deals for AI customers (its $500 billion financing partnership with six Wall Street firms was announced Monday); Meta used the structure for its data centers; Broadcom did it to help finance chips leased to Anthropic. Analysts at CreditSights warn the guarantees are "nearly costless in the boom phase, but become most relevant in a severe, abrupt downturn." What it means for us: the AI boom is partly financed with debt that only gets expensive if things go wrong. If the cycle turns, chipmakers could owe billions exactly when they're weakest — and that pressure eventually shows up in prices, cloud bills, and the economy. It's a "watch this" story, not a panic story. But it's why smart buyers don't sign multi-year AI commitments without thinking about what happens if the market cools.

**3. Google reportedly tapped AMD to help design its next AI chip.** Tom's Hardware reported, citing an analyst note from SemiAnalysis, that Google is working with AMD on its 10th-generation TPU — possibly packing CPU cores onto the chip for agent-style workloads. Neither Google nor AMD has confirmed, so treat it as a strong rumor with credible sourcing. What it means for us: every big player is trying to break Nvidia's grip on AI chips, and Google inviting AMD in signals even the biggest AI builders want cheaper, more flexible compute. More chip competition has historically meant lower prices downstream — including the API calls and cloud services small businesses buy.

Here's the deal, Reggie — two ways to wire WhatsApp into Hermes, and the number question depends on which:

**Option 1 — Baileys bridge** (`hermes whatsapp`, the quick one)
- **Self-chat mode:** uses your own number, no new number needed. You just message yourself. Good for a single-user test.
- **Bot mode:** yes, you want a **dedicated number** that isn't already registered on WhatsApp. This is a hard rule of WhatsApp itself — the account is tied to the number, and it can't already be active. Cheap options: Google Voice (free, US), a $5–15 prepaid SIM, or TextNow. Hermes explicitly recommends a separate number here because the bridge is unofficial and a ban would otherwise hit *your* number.

**Option 2 — WhatsApp Business Cloud API** (`hermes whatsapp-cloud`, the official one)
- **Yes, a dedicated business number is required** — no way around it. Plus a Meta Business account and a public HTTPS webhook URL (cloudflared tunnel on the VPS handles that free). No ban risk, but more setup and a 24-hour reply window rule.

The "new VPS" part doesn't change any of this — the number is a WhatsApp requirement, not a server one. The VPS just needs Node.js v18+ for the bridge, or a public URL for the Cloud API.

**My recommendation:** for a fresh VPS, start with the Baileys bridge in bot mode with a Google Voice or prepaid number. It's 10 minutes, no Meta paperwork, and you can switch to the Cloud API later on the same number if it becomes a real customer-facing bot.

- **CPU:** 2.5 GHz dual-core Intel Core i5-3210M (Ivy Bridge)

This is the 13-year-old Intel base unit, not an M-series. The one nice thing is the RAM is user-accessible, so 16 GB + an SSD swap gives it some life as a cheap headless box — but for anything AI/local LLM work it's basically useless (no unified memory, dual-core CPU). If you're eyeballing it for a project, tell me what you want it to do and I'll tell you straight if it's worth it.
What’s the oldest model that would work for me?

For local AI work, the cutoff is Apple Silicon — Intel Macs are dead ends for that.

**Oldest worth buying: Mac mini M1 (late 2020), 16 GB.** That's the first Apple Silicon mini, and it's still a solid local-LLM box today.

The reason is unified memory, not the chip generation. For running models, memory is what matters:
- **8 GB** — skip it, barely runs anything useful
- **16 GB** — the floor. Runs 7B–8B models comfortably in Ollama, 13B quantized is workable
- **24 GB+** — where it gets fun (bigger models, higher quality)

So the real rule isn't "oldest chip," it's "oldest Mac with 16 GB unified memory." That's an M1. And on the used market right now, a 16 GB M1 mini is the sweet spot on price — M2/M4 are faster but cost more and don't change what models you can actually fit.

Quick tiers if budget's flexible:
- **Budget pick:** M1 mini, 16 GB
- **Better:** M2/M4 mini, 16–24 GB (faster, longer macOS support)

One gotcha: the M1 mini's base config was 8 GB, so 16 GB ones are rarer on the used market — filter for it specifically. You got a use case in mind, or just price-shopping?
Does it have to be a Mac mini?

Nope. The Mac only came up because of unified memory — but it's not the only (or always the cheapest) way to run models. Three real paths:

- **Mac mini/Studio** — quiet, low power, plug-and-play, big unified memory (up to 64/128 GB on a Studio). Best when you want zero fuss and don't care about raw speed.
- **NVIDIA GPU box** — a used RTX 3090 (24 GB VRAM) is the king of price-per-performance and is 3–5× faster tokens/sec than an M-series. Downside: it's a build, plus power/noise/cooling.
- **Cloud GPU rental** (RunPod, Vast, Lambda) — no hardware at all, spin up a 24 GB GPU for ~$0.30–0.60/hr when you need it. But it's recurring spend, and you're already paying for a VPS.

What actually decides it is **what you want to run** — model size is everything here, since it sets how much memory you need, and that sets which path makes sense:

- 7–8 B models → M1/M2 mini 16 GB, or a cheap 12 GB GPU
- 13 B → 24 GB (3090, or Mac with 32 GB)
- 30–70 B → this is where Mac's big unified memory or multi-GPU earns its keep

So — what are you trying to run locally? If it's "keep Hermes + a small model humming without babysitting a GPU build," a Mac mini is honestly the turn-key answer. If you want to actually push bigger/faster inference, GPU or cloud wins.
I’d like to run the latest Qwen or similar model.
"Latest Qwen" is where size becomes the whole ballgame — let me confirm what the current lineup actually is and the memory each tier needs.

Here's the thing — "latest Qwen" is a range, and the flagship isn't a home-box model. Current lineup (as of now):

- **Qwen3.5** (Feb 2026) — the current "latest." Sizes 4B, 27B, 35B, plus a **397B MoE flagship**.
- **Qwen3.6 / 3.8 27B** — the hot local-default right now.

The 397B flagship needs ~200 GB of memory — that's cloud or a multi-GPU server, not something you buy. But the **27B tier is the real answer**: it's current-gen, dramatically smarter than anything you're running CPU-only now, and it fits one affordable box.

Memory math at Q4 quantization:
| Model size | Memory needed | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| 4–8 B | ~5–8 GB | 16 GB Mac / 12 GB GPU |
| **27 B** (Qwen3.5/3.6) | **~17 GB** | **24 GB GPU (3090) / 32 GB Mac** |
| 35 B | ~22 GB | 24 GB tight, 32 GB better |
| 72 B | ~40 GB | 48 GB (2×24 GB) / 64 GB Mac Studio |
| 397 B MoE | ~200 GB | cloud / server only |

So my recommendation: **target the 27B tier**, and it comes down to one fork:

- **Used RTX 3090 (24 GB)** — best price-per-performance, ~38 tok/s, but it's a build (power, cooling, a box to put it in).
- **32 GB Mac** (M4 mini 32 GB, or a Studio) — turn-key, quiet, no fuss, just slower tokens/sec.

Either one runs the latest Qwen 27B comfortably. The only real decision is speed-and-tinkering (GPU) vs plug-and-play (Mac). Which one's you?
What are the costs?
Let me pull current pricing so I'm not guessing — the card, the Macs, and cloud for comparison.

Here's the honest money picture (current, Aug 2026):

**The turn-key Mac path**
| Option | Price | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| M4 mini 24 GB | $799 | too tight for 27B — skip |
| **M4 mini 32 GB** | **$999** | **27B Q4 comfortable — the sweet spot** |
| M4 Pro mini 48 GB | $1,799 | faster + headroom |
| Mac Studio M4 Max 64 GB | ~$2,499 | 72B territory |

**The GPU path** (needs a whole box — you're CPU-only, so it's not just the card)
| Item | Price |
|---|---|
| Used RTX 3090 24 GB | ~$1,000 (used to be $600, AI demand shot it up) |
| PSU + case + CPU/RAM/mobo | +$400–600 |
| **Total** | **~$1,400–1,600** |

**Cloud** — 24 GB GPU ~$0.30–0.40/hr. Light use (few hrs/day) ≈ $30–60/mo. 24/7 ≈ $220–290/mo. Zero upfront.

**My call:** M4 mini 32 GB at $999 is your answer. The 3090 used to be the steal, but at ~$1,000 *plus* a build it's now more expensive and more tinkering than a Mac that just works — and I know you don't want a build.

One honest caveat before you buy: a 27B model on the M4 mini runs ~7–10 tokens/sec (its 120 GB/s memory bandwidth is the limiter), vs ~38 tok/s on a 3090. That's fine for your actual use — agentic/Hermes/cron/drafting work, not staring at a chat window. But if you ever want snappy interactive chat on a big model, the M4 Pro mini (48 GB, ~2× bandwidth) is the upgrade worth the extra $800.

Net: **$999, M4 mini 32 GB, done.** Want me to dig up a specific listing, or is this still price-shopping?
That’s still too much. Maybe after I close a few AI CoS clients

Good call — don't buy hardware on spec. That's a "money's in the bank" purchase, not a "hoping to close" one.

Meanwhile, the zero-upfront version is renting: spin up a 24 GB GPU on RunPod or Vast for ~$0.30–0.40/hr only when you actually need a big model, and kill it when you're done. Costs you a few bucks on the days you use it, nothing to own or babysit. Everything else keeps running on what you've got.

- **After a couple CoS clients close** — M4 mini 32 GB ($999) and never think about it again

Any idea what the specs would be for this Mac mini?

Mac mini serial number C07K14DCDWYL
I can decode that. Let me verify the details before I give you specs.

Decoded it. That serial is the old 12-character Apple format, and the 4th character "K" puts manufacture in the first week of January 2013 — so this is a **Mac mini (Late 2012)**, the Intel Ivy Bridge model. It's one of two configs (the serial alone won't tell me which):

**Mac mini (Late 2012) — Macmini6,1**
- 2.5 GHz dual-core Intel Core i5 (Turbo to 3.1 GHz), 3MB L3
- Intel HD Graphics 4000 (512MB shared)
- 4GB DDR3-1600 (upgradeable to 16GB)
- 500GB 5400rpm SATA hard drive

**Mac mini (Late 2012) — Macmini6,2**
- 2.3 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7 (Turbo to 3.3 GHz), 6MB L3
- Intel HD Graphics 4000
- 4GB DDR3-1600 (upgradeable to 16GB)
- 1TB 5400rpm SATA hard drive (server variant: dual 1TB drives)

Both share:
- 4× USB 3.0, Thunderbolt, HDMI, FireWire 800, SDXC slot, Gigabit Ethernet
- 802.11n Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 4.0
- Shipped with OS X 10.8 Mountain Lion; tops out at **macOS 10.15 Catalina**

Head's up: this thing is 13 years old, and Apple dropped software support after Catalina — so it's genuinely dated now, not a "retro but fine" machine. If you're eyeing it for anything beyond a light fileserver/media box, I'd steer you toward an M-series mini instead.

To pin down the exact config, check Apple menu → About This Mac (or run `system_profiler SPHardwareDataType`), which shows the processor and model identifier directly.

## ✅ Voice TTS endpoint — running on your VPS

**URL:** `http://100.90.111.113:8030` (Tailscale)

| Method | Path | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/health` | Model + readiness + voice list |
| GET | `/voices` | The 9 preset voices |
| POST | `/tts` | `{"text":"...", "voice":"ryan", "format":"mp3"}` → returns `job_id` |
| GET | `/tts/{job_id}` | Poll status → `done` + `audio_url` |
| GET | `/tts/{job_id}/audio` | The rendered audio file |

**Verified end-to-end:** submitted a job with `"voice":"ryan"`, got a 6.2s MP3 back. Error handling tested (bad voice → 400, empty text → 400, bad job → 404).

**Running as:** `voice-tts.service` — `enabled` (starts on boot) + `active` + `Restart=always`. Model warm-loads in ~7s at boot.

## How a PWA hits it (the "Phil speaks" path)

```bash
# 1. ask for audio
curl -X POST http://100.90.111.113:8030/tts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"text":"Your meeting is at 1pm. Want a briefing?","voice":"ryan","format":"mp3"}'
# → {"job_id":"...","poll_url":"/tts/..."}

# 2. poll until status=done (takes ~2.5 min on this CPU)
curl -s http://100.90.111.113:8030/tts/<job_id>

# 3. play the audio
curl -o reply.mp3 http://100.90.111.113:8030/tts/<job_id>/audio
```

The async queue is the whole point — since each line takes ~2.5 min, the PWA posts, polls in the background, and plays the audio when it's ready (not a blocking request that would time out).

## Two things to flag

1. **No auth right now.** It's bound to `0.0.0.0`, so anything on your Tailscale network can generate audio. When you expose this to a real PWA, set `TTS_API_KEY` in `/etc/systemd/system/voice-tts.service` (the server already checks it via `X-API-Key` header). Say the word and I'll lock it down.

2. **Voice-clone mode isn't wired yet** — this endpoint uses the 9 preset voices. The 3-second voice clone (Base model) is a separate toggle I can add when you want Phil to sound like a specific voice.

What is the idea behind creating a new profile on here?

A profile is a completely separate instance of me. Same software, but its own brain — its own memory, its own skills, its own sessions, its own config, its own bot token. Nothing leaks between them.

Think of it like this: right now you're talking to the `default` profile — that's "your Phil." It knows your family, your Gmail, your pricing, your daily AM checks. All that context is here.

A new profile is a second Phil that knows *nothing* about you unless I write it in. It lives at `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>/` with its own copy of everything.

Why you'd do that:

**1. Keep client conversations separate.** The big one. When a prospect does a discovery call, you don't want their business details polluting *your* CoS's memory, and you don't want your personal stuff leaking to them. A dedicated profile gives the prospect their own CoS that only knows what it should.

**2. Different identities/brands.** BizGrowth CoS and NextCap CoS are the same agent but different voices, different SOUL.md, different bot names. Each brand gets its own profile.

**3. Different jobs that shouldn't mix.** One profile for daily ops, one for a specific client, one for demos — each keeps its own memory clean so the agent doesn't confuse "Reggie's pricing" with "the prospect's insurance agency."

**4. Safety.** If a client's bot goes sideways or gets spammed, you kill that profile without touching your main one.

That's exactly what `nextcap-prospect-demo` does — spins up a fresh `<brand>-cos` profile per demo so a prospect's discovery call never contaminates your daily driver.

You asking because you're thinking of a new one, or just want to understand it?
OK. So what if I set up a totally different profile for a family member? Will she have her own login and can she rename her own AI Agent?

Short answer: yes, she gets her own totally separate agent — but "login" here doesn't mean what you're probably picturing. Let me clear it up.

**Her "login" = a chat surface, not a server account.**

The profile lives on *your* VPS. She never touches the server, never has a password, never logs into Hermes itself. What she gets is her own way to talk to it — the cleanest being her own Telegram bot:

- You make a new bot in BotFather (e.g. `@TiffanyCoSBot`)
- She messages it from her own phone
- That's it. That's her whole "login." She opens Telegram and talks.

No shared memory with your Phil, no shared sessions, no seeing your stuff. Complete wall between you.

**Can she rename her agent? Kind of — but not through a self-serve screen.**

- What she *calls* it — absolutely, it's just what she types. If she wants to call it "Gloria" instead of "Phil," she just does.
- The bot's display name — set by you in BotFather. You can change it anytime, but she can't change the username herself (BotFather is on your Telegram account).
- The agent's actual identity (what it calls *itself*, its personality, its voice) — that lives in a `SOUL.md` file on the server. She can ask it to "go by Gloria" mid-chat and it'll roll with it for that conversation, but a *persistent* rename is a one-line file edit I do.

So the honest version: **she doesn't get a login screen or a settings dashboard.** She gets a private chat with an agent whose name and personality you (or I) set. If she wants to rename it, you tell me and I flip it in 30 seconds.

The upside of this setup is exactly what you want for family — it's turn-key for *her*. She just talks. Nothing to install, no account to manage, no way for her to break it.

Want me to set it up? If so, two quick things: which family member, and does she want it on Telegram (easiest) or somewhere else like iMessage?
so she uses all my API keys? If she wanted to set up her Google stuff like email and calendar and such, you would be able to help her?

Two separate things there — let me split them, because the answers are different.

**Your API keys — not "all" of them, but yes, your bill.**

Each profile gets its *own* `.env` file, so I scope what it has. She doesn't automatically inherit every key on your server — I'd give her profile only the model key it needs (DeepSeek, etc.) and nothing else. No Gmail, no LinkedIn, no MCP secrets, none of that.

But here's the honest part: whatever *is* in there is still **your** account. Her chats burn **your** token spend. Hermes has no per-user billing — it's one server, one set of keys, one bill. And no, she can't see or copy the keys themselves; she just uses them.

So: isolated *brain*, shared *wallet*. For a family member that's almost certainly fine, but you should know that's the deal.

**Her Google stuff — yes, and this is the clean part.**

Her profile can connect to **her own** Google account via OAuth, completely separate from yours. She logs in as herself (her own Gmail), and then her agent reads *her* email, *her* calendar, *her* Drive. Your Google stays walled off.

So the setup ends up like:
- Model/API keys → yours, shared bill
- Google (email, calendar, Drive) → hers, her own account
- Memory, sessions, agent identity → hers, isolated profile
- Access → just her Telegram bot on her phone

One honest caveat to flag: everything runs on your VPS, so her conversation transcripts technically live on your server and you *could* read them. For a spouse that's a non-issue, just being straight with you about where the data sits.

The Google hookup is a known flow (headless OAuth for the VPS + multi-account). I can do it end to end.

So the real question before I build anything: **is this for Tiffany, and does she want email/calendar day one or just the chat agent first?**

I'm thinking about it for her because she/we have a lot of stuff going on and I think she needs a personal assistant.
question: would she be able to switch models like I can?

Technically yes, but only within the box you build for her — and honestly, you probably shouldn't hand her that control.

**How it works.** Model switching is a `/model` slash command (and there's a picker in the desktop app). Since those commands surface through Telegram too, she *could* type `/model` and pick. But two catches:

1. She can only choose from models **you've already wired into her profile's config** — your providers, your keys. She can't add her own key or pick some random model. Her universe is whatever you pre-approve.
2. On Telegram it's clunky — she'd be picking from a list of model names she doesn't care about, not a nice dropdown.

**My pushback:** don't give Tiffany model switching. It's a power-user footgun. A non-technical user will either ignore it or accidentally flip to a slower/dumber/dearer model and not know why her assistant "got weird." She doesn't want a config panel — she wants an assistant that just answers.

The right setup is: **you (or I) pick one solid default for her profile and lock it.** If she ever says "this seems slow" or "it keeps getting this wrong," that's a signal to *me*, not a setting for *her*. I flip it in 30 seconds and she never notices the difference.

That's the actual product decision here: she gets a personal assistant, not a Hermes install. You keep the knobs, she gets the output.

So — default plan for Tiffany, if you want it:

- Own profile + own Telegram bot (her "login")
- One locked model, good default
- Her own Google (email/calendar) connected via OAuth
- Memory/personality tuned to her, separate from yours
- You control any changes

Want me to start building that, or still in the "thinking it over" phase?
still thinking it over

All good. No rush — it's a real thing to think through, especially the shared-bill piece.

Whenever you're ready, the setup's about 20 minutes of my time and it's all reversible — profile can be deleted cleanly if she doesn't take to it.

One thing to mull: the honest questions to settle before building are just **which chat surface she'd actually use** (Telegram's the easy one, iMessage is possible but fiddlier) and **whether she wants email/calendar from day one or starts with a plain chat assistant.** That's the whole decision, really.

Ping me when you want to move.
Let's go ahead and create a profile for Tiffany

## The setup in one line

**"Hermes" is a robot contact inside Google Chat, and that robot is me.** When you DM the robot, your message comes to me (Phil), and I answer back through the robot. That's it. The robot is a separate thing from *your* Google Chat account.

Think of it like this: the robot is its own phone number. People message the robot, I pick up. Your personal Google Chat is a *different* phone — I don't touch that one.

## Your three questions

**1. "Can I send a direct message to someone using Google Chat?"**

Two ways to read this:

- **You** (Reggie the human) DMing someone from the Google Chat app — **yes**, that's a normal Google Chat feature. Click "New chat," type their email. Has nothing to do with me or the bot.
- **Me** (the bot) sending a message to someone on your behalf — **no.** A bot can only talk inside a chat where *someone already messaged it first*. It can't cold-message a person.

**2. "Can I reply to someone who's sent me a message in Google Chat?"**

Depends on *where* they messaged you:

| Where they messaged you | Can I see it / reply? |
|---|---|
| They DM'd the **Hermes robot** | ✅ Yes — that's the whole feature |
| They DM'd **your** Google Chat ([EMAIL]) | ❌ No — that's your personal inbox, not the bot's |

So: if someone messages *you* normally in Google Chat, I don't see it and can't reply. Only messages sent to the **Hermes bot** reach me.

**3. "How does this work?"**

```
You DM "Hermes" bot  →  Google  →  my gateway  →  me (Phil)  →  I answer  →  back through the bot  →  your DM
```

It's just a chat room between you and me, living inside Google Chat.

## `agency-agents-router` — what it actually is

Not a build tool. It's a **persona router** for a 270-agent "Agency" roster sitting in a 3.9 MB JSON file. It registers 4 tools:

| Tool | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `agency_agents_search` | keyword-search the roster |
| `agency_agents_inspect` | read one specialist's metadata |
| `agency_agents_load` | inject that specialist's *personality prompt* into the current turn |
| `agency_agents_delegate` | hand the task to `delegate_task` with the persona as context |

The roster is a grab-bag of role-play specialists across 17 divisions:

- **engineering (58)** — code reviewer, backend architect, data engineer, etc.
- **specialized (57)** — misc niche roles
- **marketing (36)**, **game-development (21)**, **gis (13)**, **security (12)**, **design (10)**, **sales (9)**, **testing (9)**...
- down to **healthcare (3)**

Some are legit (Code Reviewer, Backend Architect). A lot are niche personas — Anthropologist, Geographer, Whimsy Injector, Image Prompt Engineer. It's the "The Agency" multi-agent persona pack.

- **code-bridge** → routes work to **real coding CLIs** (Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Gemini). Separate agents, actual execution, real git/test output. That's a build tool.
- **agency-agents-router** → loads a **personality prompt** into the same session. No separate execution — it's prompt-flavored context, not a platform.

They look similar ("decide who handles the task") but they're completely different mechanisms. Your instinct is correct — **for building, code-bridge is the one.**

does chatgpt store all my memories?

Short answer: no, not everything.

ChatGPT has a "memory" feature, but it's selective, not a full transcript of your life. Here's how it actually works:

- **What gets saved** — facts it thinks are worth keeping (your name, job, preferences, projects) plus anything you explicitly say "remember this." It does *not* store every word of every chat as a "memory."
- **Chat history ≠ memory** — your actual conversations are saved separately as history. Memory is the cross-chat stuff (the "Reggie lives in Phoenix, works on X" type facts).
- **You control it** — Settings → Personalization → Memory shows you every individual memory, and you can delete any of them one by one, or wipe the whole thing.
- **You can turn it off** — flip memory off entirely, or use a Temporary Chat (the little toggle when you start a new chat) and it remembers nothing and doesn't even save the chat.
- **Data training** — unless you opt out (Settings → Data controls → "Improve the model for everyone"), chats can be used to train the model. That's separate from the memory feature.

So: it remembers *highlights*, not everything, and you can see and delete every bit of it.

One thing worth flagging — this is different from **me**. My memory (what I know about you — Ian's recruiting site, BizGrowthAI, the daily AM checks, etc.) lives on your own VPS, not on OpenAI's servers. It's yours, it's local, and you've got full control over it.

Want me to walk you through where to check/manage the ChatGPT memory settings, or were you asking because you're worried about privacy there specifically?

- GPU instances are **pricey**: A100 80GB ~$3–4+/hr, H100 ~$5–8+/hr on-demand.
- You usually need **quota approval** before AWS/GCP will even give you a GPU instance on a fresh account.
- Billing is per-second/hour, no commit, so technically pay-as-you-go — but the per-hour GPU cost is the worst of the options.

Voice chat is actually three services glued together, and the LLM is only one of them:

1. **STT** — your speech → text (Whisper, Deepgram, AssemblyAI)
2. **LLM** — text → text ← *this* is the piece you were asking about renting a GPU for
3. **TTS** — text → speech (ElevenLabs, Cartesia, OpenAI, or free Edge TTS)

...plus a **realtime transport** layer (WebRTC/WebSocket) so all three stream without 2–3 seconds of dead air between "you talk" and "it talks back."

The thing most people get wrong: **for voice, the LLM is usually not what makes it feel fast or cheap.** STT + TTS latency and the streaming are. A fast API model (Groq/OpenAI) replies in ~300ms; a self-hosted model on a rented GPU adds another 300ms–1s+ unless you tune it. So self-hosting an open model is a *later* optimization, not step one.

Three ways to build it, in order of effort:

**Tier 1 — managed voice platform (fastest, least work).** Vapi, Retell, or LiveKit Cloud at ~$0.05–0.15/min. They handle STT + LLM + TTS + WebRTC + even phone calls. You just bring your system prompt. Best for "voice in three apps this month."

**Tier 2 — LiveKit self-hosted + your own stack.** LiveKit Agents (open source) gives you the realtime transport + orchestration for free; you wire in Deepgram (STT) + your LLM + ElevenLabs/Cartesia (TTS). Full control, runs on your box, more moving parts.

**Tier 3 — fully self-hosted.** LiveKit + faster-whisper (you already run this inside Hermes) + an open LLM on a rented GPU + open TTS. Cheapest per-token at scale, most ops, and the latency needs real tuning to feel conversational.

My read: start Tier 1 or 2 with an **API LLM**, get voice live in *one* app first, then swap in a self-hosted model later only if per-token cost or data privacy forces it. Self-hosting day one will slow you down and won't make the voice feel any faster.

Read the whole repo — it's legit and well-built (1.7k stars, updated yesterday). But I'll give you the honest verdict before you get excited: **it won't run on your hardware.**

## What it is
A thin harness that lets an agent drive a **real iPhone** — open apps, tap, type, swipe, read the screen — by controlling the Mac's iPhone Mirroring window. OCR for "eyes," synthetic mouse/keyboard for "hands." No jailbreak, no Xcode. Clean design, ~500-line core, stateless.

## Can Hermes drive it? Yes, in principle
It's agent-agnostic — just a CLI plus a skill file. It registers the same way with Claude Code or Codex, so Hermes could call `phone-harness` exactly the same. That part is not the problem.

## The blocker: it's macOS-only
The entire trick rides on **iPhone Mirroring, which is macOS Sequoia+**. Install requirements are unambiguous:
- A Mac on the **same Apple ID** as the phone
- Phone **physically near** the Mac (Mirroring is proximity-based)
- macOS-only libraries (`pyobjc` + Quartz/Vision/AppKit)

You've got Windows (Yoga) + iPhone + a Linux VPS. No Mac. So today there's no path — iPhone Mirroring simply doesn't exist on Windows or Linux.

## What it'd actually take to use it
A Mac mini (M4, ~$599) sitting on your desk, paired to your iPhone via Mirroring. Then Hermes (your VPS) SSHs into the Mac over Tailscale and drives the phone through it. Totally doable, adds one box to your setup.

## One thing to flag
This is **screen control**, not voice. If your real goal is the voice-chat integration we were just talking about, this tool doesn't do phone calls or audio at all — it's for automating the phone UI (opening apps, tapping, typing). Different problem.

So the decision that matters: are you trying to **control your iPhone's screen** from an agent, or trying to **put voice chat in your apps**? Reviewed the repo end to end — homepage, services page, both free tools, the blog, and the brand tokens in `globals.css`. I also pulled your existing BizGrowthAI brand kit and past IG work. Here's the full picture and the strategy.

## What the repo already tells us (this is your content spine)

BizGrowthAI's positioning is unusually clean, and it's *already* a content strategy:

- **"Practical AI for real businesses." "Make AI useful for your business."** No hype, no technical maze.
- **"Built for busy owners, not AI experts."**
- Three jobs-to-be-done everywhere on the site: **win back time / market consistently / serve customers better.**
- The blog's one post — *"When every AI tool looks the same"* — is your best asset. Its thesis is the whole brand: **"the hard part isn't the tool anymore, it's everything around it — choosing, implementing, building the habit."**

That's the differentiator in a crowded AI-tips space. Everyone posts "10 AI tools to know." Almost no one posts *"you don't need 47 tools — here's the one task to automate first."* Lean into that.

Your current IG is running "AI news for sales pros" daily briefs. This strategy **evolves that, doesn't replace it** — news becomes one pillar, reframed as "what it means for you," and we make the *tip* the lead pillar.

---

## The strategy

**Positioning:** Be the practical friend, not the AI guru. Every post answers one question — *"what's one thing I can actually do this week?"* — in plain English.

**Voice rules (non-negotiable, from your existing brand):**
- Casual, human-to-owner. No jargon, no hype words ("revolutionary," "game-changer").
- No emojis. No hashtags on IG, FB, or LinkedIn. TikTok is the one exception — 4–6 hashtags only (it's how TikTok discovery works), still no emojis.
- Lead with the takeaway, end with an open question to drive comments.
- Always the "what it means for you" angle.

### 5 content pillars

| Pillar | % | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quick tip / "try this"** | 40% | One concrete prompt or workflow, usable today | "Here's the exact prompt to turn a meeting note into an action list" |
| **News → what it means** | 20% | One AI story, stripped of hype, practical takeaway | "Siri got smarter — here's what that actually changes for you" |
| **No-hype myth-busting** | 15% | Kill a fear or a false promise | "AI won't replace your marketing team. It will replace the 20 minutes you lose on follow-ups." |
| **Show your work** | 15% | Before/after of a real workflow | "Lead response: 3 missed leads/mo → answered in 2 min, 24/7" |
| **Engagement** | 10% | Polls, questions, "what's eating your time?" | "What's the one task you dread repeating every week?" |

Pillar 1 is your bread and butter — that's the "smart AI tips" you asked for, and it's what drives saves and follows.

---

## Platform playbook

| Platform | Format | Cadence | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LinkedIn (company page)** | Text-first posts + PDF carousels | 3x/week | Longest copy. Bare URLs on their own line (no markdown). End with a question. |
| **Instagram (@bizgrowthai)** | Reels + 4:5 carousels | 3–4x/week | Educational carousels are your highest-save format. No hashtags/emojis. |
| **Facebook** | LinkedIn posts repurposed, slightly warmer | 3x/week | Link goes in the caption (allowed on FB). No hashtags/emojis. |
| **TikTok** | 9:16, 30–45s vertical | 3x/week | First line must stop the scroll. Text-on-screen or face-to-camera. 4–6 hashtags (#smallbusiness #learnontiktok #techtok #aitips). No emojis. |

### The repurposing engine (this is what makes it turn-key)

**One idea → four posts.** Don't create 12 separate ideas a week. Create 3, and repurpose each across platforms:

```
One "AI tip" idea
  ├─ LinkedIn:  text post (the tip + why it matters + question)
  ├─ Instagram: 4:5 carousel (5 slides: hook → the problem → the prompt → the result → CTA)
  ├─ Facebook:  same carousel + warm caption with the free-tool link
  └─ TikTok:    30s vertical — hook line → on-screen steps → "save this" CTA
```

That's 3 ideas → 12 posts a week, with maybe 30 minutes of adaptation. It also *demonstrates* your own "content engine" service without ever pitching it.

---

## Weekly rhythm (sample)

| Day | LinkedIn | IG | FB | TikTok |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | Quick tip (text) | Tip carousel | Repost carousel | Tip video |
| Tue | — | Story poll | — | — |
| Wed | News → what it means | News carousel | Repost | News video |
| Thu | Myth-bust (text) | Reel (tip) | Repost | — |
| Fri | Show your work | Carousel | Repost | Show-your-work video |
| Sat | — | Story + engage 20 accts | — | — |

---

## First batch — 10 ready-to-go ideas

1. **The follow-up prompt** — paste a customer's question, get a reply in your voice in 2 minutes.
2. **"You don't need 47 AI tools"** — the commoditization take, short-form.
3. **Meeting notes → action list** — the exact 3-line prompt.
4. **One idea → a week of content** — your literal content-engine pitch, shown as a tip.
5. **"AI wrote something generic — here's why"** — the context lesson (your prompt builder demo).
6. **Answer your FAQ once, personalize forever** — response library tip.
7. **"What's the one task you dread every week?"** — engagement post.
8. **News → what it means** — one fresh AI headline, stripped.
9. **"AI won't replace you. The owner using AI will."** — myth-bust, but soft (you know the audience).
10. **Before/after: onboarding cut 60%** — show-your-work with a real metric.

**News → what it means (IG carousel cover):**

---

## Guardrails (what to keep quiet)

- **No consultant/referral program** — agreed, and the strategy doesn't need it. If anyone asks in comments, answer in DMs, not publicly.
- **No pricing, no "hire us."** Soft CTAs only: the free Prompt Builder, the free Opportunity Map, the two free PDFs, and "follow for more."

messages.content: in terms of the soulprint extension can you give me the best way to explain the differences between: API, MCP, and plugin?
Let me pull the SoulPrint skill first so I ground this in your actual architecture, not generic definitions.

Got it — grounded in how SoulPrint actually works (three repos: engine, MCP server, Chrome extension), not textbook definitions. Here's the clean way to explain it.

## The core mental model

**Same engine, three doors.** SoulPrint's brain lives at `soulprintengine.ai`. API, MCP, and the extension are just three different ways to reach it — none of them is a separate product.

- **API = the engine itself**
- **MCP = how AI talks to it**
- **Plugin/extension = how your browser uses it**

---

## The 10-second version (when someone asks on the spot)

> "They're all the same SoulPrint engine underneath. The **API** is the raw engine — you send it a request, it sends data back. **MCP** is the standard language that lets any AI assistant discover and use that engine without a human hand-writing each request. The **extension** is the resident helper that lives in your browser and injects your SoulPrint into ChatGPT or Claude while you're chatting. MCP and the extension both sit on top of the API."

---

## The full explanation (ready to paste / hand off)

**1. API — the raw engine.** A set of doors with clear labels. A developer sends a direct request — "give me my memories" — and gets a structured response back. Precise and fast, but you have to know the exact address and format every time. This is the foundation everything else is built on.

**2. MCP — the universal AI adapter.** MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a shared standard, like a common language for AI tools. Our MCP server wraps the API so that *any* MCP-compatible AI — Claude Code, Cursor, Hermes — can automatically discover what SoulPrint can do and use it, without a human writing custom code for each tool. Write it once, it works everywhere.

**3. Plugin/extension — the resident helper.** This one doesn't wait to be called. It lives in the browser, watches you chat in ChatGPT or Claude, and quietly injects your memories and identity context into the conversation as you go. No requests, no setup per session — it just does the work in the background.

---

## Cheat sheet (one line each)

| | What it is | Who uses it |
|---|---|---|
| **API** | Raw engine — request in, data out | Developers |
| **MCP** | Standard adapter so AI can use the engine | AI agents (Claude, Cursor, Hermes) |
| **Extension** | In-browser helper that injects context live | End users chatting in ChatGPT/Claude |

---

## The "aha" line that clears up confusion

**The API is the foundation. MCP and the extension are two different ways of consuming the same API** — one for AI assistants, one for humans in the browser. People get stuck thinking they're competing or parallel products; they're not. They're the same engine wearing different front doors.

---

**The research, straight up:** the strongest study on this topic (Gerlich 2025) actually argues the *opposite* — heavy AI use can weaken critical thinking. So I didn't fight it, I used it. The nuance in that study is the whole ballgame: the problem is *trust* (blindly accepting output), not *use*. That's exactly your point, and it's backed by two other real sources: Risko & Gilbert's foundational "cognitive offloading" paper (2016) — offloading routine load frees working memory for higher-order thinking — and this year's APA finding that structured AI use *preserves* your abilities. **The post:**

Hot take: AI is making my critical thinking better, not worse.

My brain has run at a million miles an hour for as long as I can remember. Most of you who've worked with me know this. Probably undiagnosed ADHD, honestly.

Since I started building and focusing with AI, that changed. I'm not holding the small stuff in my head anymore, so I finally have room to actually think.

There's a word for it: cognitive offloading. When you move routine mental load onto a tool, you free up working memory for higher-order thinking. Risko and Gilbert wrote the foundational paper on this back in 2016 — years before most people touched a transformer.

The "AI is making us dumber" people usually cite Gerlich's 2025 study. Fair. But read it closely: the problem he found is trust, not use. People who blindly accept whatever the model spits out do get weaker. People who treat AI as a thinking partner don't.

So no, AI isn't rotting anyone's brain. The people saying that just aren't using it right. They're outsourcing their thinking instead of upgrading it.

The tool isn't the problem. The posture is.

- `dist/topics.json` and `unified_topics.json` match byte-for-byte (5,456,949 bytes)
- Git working tree clean; `a2d1371 cron: refresh topic dashboard data` is now on `origin/main`
- GitHub Action will pick up the `data/` commit and rebuild the public `topics.json`
