topics.name: Building AI Agent Mobile App for DisciplinedOS

sessions.title: Building AI Agent Mobile App for DisciplinedOS

messages.content:
i think i have a big ask: Can you take a look at my repo coolgeekme/DisciplinedOS and figure out whether or not it would be possible to build a native iOS and Android mobile app where the user would use the app like an AI Agent in regards to communicating like texting or voice chat and the app would be able to determine whether or not the contents/context of that communication exchange would be worth entering into the Disciplined OS platform?

Basically, I'm looking for a true personal and professional Chief of Staff AI Agent where the user can communicate anything and then be able to log into DisciplinedOS.com and view the important information based on what the Chief of Staff deemend important.

Does that make sense?
Makes total sense — you're describing a capture layer (chat/voice agent) that feeds a curated system-of-record (DisciplinedOS). Let me look at the repo first to see what we're working with.

Yes — it makes complete sense, and after digging through the repo I have good news: **this is very feasible, and you're closer than you probably think.** The backend is already ~70% of an agent platform. Here's my assessment.

## What DisciplinedOS already has (this is the big deal)

I cloned it to `~/DisciplinedOS-inspect` and traced the server code:

- **A full AI function-calling surface** — `server/ai-tools.ts` (1,600 lines) already defines ~30 agent tools: `create_task`, `create_idea`, `create_lead`, `create_contact`, `create_note`, `create_deal`, `record_payment`, `search_across_all`, etc. This *is* the "Chief of Staff hands" — the machinery that writes deemed-important info into the platform already exists.
- **AI quick-add** — `POST /api/quick-add` (routes.ts:5786) already does natural-language → classified entity creation.
- **Voice pipeline** — `POST /api/voice-transcribe` + audio upload endpoints with Whisper transcription and GPT summaries → notes. The "talk to it" path exists server-side.
- **Token-based API auth** — Firebase Auth with Bearer ID tokens (`firebaseAuth.ts`). That's exactly what a mobile app needs; no session/cookie rework required.
- **AI insights scanning** (`aiInsightsService.ts`) — the seed of the "what's important" judgment layer.

So the ask isn't "build an AI agent platform" — it's **build a mobile capture client + a triage brain on top of an agent backend that already exists.**

## What's missing (the actual build)

**1. The mobile app itself.** My strong recommendation: **React Native (Expo)**, not separate Swift/Kotlin apps. Your stack is already TypeScript/React, Firebase Auth has first-class RN support, you get iOS + Android from one codebase, native mic/push/background audio, and Expo's EAS handles App Store/Play Store builds. "True native" x2 codebases would double cost for zero user-visible benefit here. (A cheaper stopgap — Capacitor-wrapping the existing PWA — gets you in the stores fast but makes the conversational/voice UX second-class; I'd skip it for this vision.)

**2. The Chief of Staff triage layer** — the piece that makes this different from the existing assistant. A new endpoint like `POST /api/chief-of-staff/message` that:
- Accepts any message (text, or voice → existing Whisper transcription)
- Runs a **triage pass**: "Is anything in this exchange worth persisting? Which entities — task, idea, lead, contact, deal activity, note? What's the significance score?"
- Calls the *existing* ai-tools functions to write the important stuff
- Replies conversationally either way (it's still a chat — most messages won't create records, and that's fine)

**3. A review/inbox surface on DisciplinedOS.com** — "Here's what your CoS logged this week" with confirm/edit/dismiss. This feedback loop is what makes the "deemed important" judgment trustworthy and trainable (dismissals become few-shot examples of what *not* to log).

**4. Conversation memory** — a `conversations` collection in Firestore so the CoS has continuity across sessions ("that plumber lead I mentioned Tuesday").

**5. Voice chat depth** — v1: push-to-talk → Whisper → text reply (all plumbing exists). v2: OpenAI Realtime API for true full-duplex voice conversation. Don't start with v2.

## Rough phasing

| Phase | Scope | Effort ballpark |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Expo app: Firebase login, chat UI, push-to-talk voice, hits existing endpoints | 2–3 weeks |
| 2 | CoS triage endpoint + conversation memory + significance scoring | 1–2 weeks |
| 3 | Web review inbox + push notifications ("I logged 3 things from today") | 1 week |
| 4 | Realtime voice, proactive briefings, calendar-aware nudges | ongoing |

One honest caveat: App Store review for AI chat apps is routine now, but you'll need the Apple $99/yr dev account, privacy policy (you have one), and mic-usage descriptions — all standard.

Want me to go a level deeper on any of this — e.g., sketch the CoS triage endpoint design against your actual schema, or scaffold the Expo app? Also: should I keep the `~/DisciplinedOS-inspect` clone around for follow-up work, or clean it up?
I would love you to sketch the CoS triage endpoint design against the actual schema
Let me look at the actual schema and the quick-add/ai-tools internals so the design matches reality.

I traced the real internals — key facts the design leans on:

- `storage` is **Firestore** (`storage.ts:2130` → `export const storage = firebaseStorage`); the Drizzle schema is the type layer. So "new tables" = new Firestore collections + types in `shared/schema.ts`.
- `executeAITool(toolName, args, userId)` in `ai-tools.ts:745` is already a clean, user-scoped dispatcher — the CoS can call it directly, zero duplication.
- `callOpenAIWithLogging(...)` gives you per-feature cost tracking for free in the admin dashboard.
- `aiInsights` already has `isDismissed` / `isActioned` / `relatedEntityType` / `relatedEntityId` — which means **the review-inbox storage already exists**.

Here's the sketch:

---

## CoS Triage Endpoint — Design

### New file: `server/chiefOfStaff.ts`, mounted in `routes.ts`

```
POST /api/cos/message            ← the main endpoint
GET  /api/cos/captures?status=pending
POST /api/cos/captures/:id/confirm
POST /api/cos/captures/:id/dismiss
```

All behind the existing `isAuthenticated` (Firebase Bearer token → `req.user.uid`), so the mobile app auths exactly like the PWA.

### Request / Response

```ts
// POST /api/cos/message
{
  conversationId?: string,   // omit → creates one (reuses existing conversations/messages collections)
  text?: string,             // OR:
  recordingId?: string       // voice path: app hits /api/voice-transcribe first, passes transcript through
}

// Response
{
  conversationId: string,
  reply: string,                      // conversational answer — it's still a chat
  captures: [{
    id: string,
    action: "created" | "updated" | "proposed",
    entityType: "task" | "idea" | "lead" | "contact" | "note" | "deal_activity" | "contact_note",
    entityId?: string,                // set when auto-executed
    title: string,                    // "Task: Follow up with Rogers RV on invoice"
    significance: number,             // 0–1
    sourceExcerpt: string             // the sentence(s) that triggered it
  }]
}
```

The `captures` array is what lets the mobile app render "📌 Logged: …" chips under the reply — immediate, glanceable feedback that the CoS did something.

### The pipeline (one handler, three stages)

**Stage 1 — cheap significance gate.** Most messages ("lol ok", "what's the weather") shouldn't pay for a GPT-5 tool loop. One call to **Gemini 2.5 Flash** (already a provider in this repo) with the last ~6 messages of context:

```
Does this exchange contain anything worth persisting to the user's
business/life OS? Categories: commitment/action item, new person or
lead, money/deal event, idea, durable fact worth remembering.
Return {capture_worthy: bool, confidence: 0-1, categories: [...]}
```

Not capture-worthy → skip to Stage 3 (just reply). This mirrors the intent-check pattern `quick-add` already uses at routes.ts:5786, but with a cheaper model — and every call is cost-tagged via `callOpenAIWithLogging` with `feature: "cos_gate"`, so your admin dashboard shows exactly what the gate costs.

**Stage 2 — tool loop (GPT-5, only when gated in).** Reuse `AI_TOOLS` filtered to a curated subset — the CoS should *not* get all ~30 tools:

- **Read (dedup + context):** `search_across_all`, `get_projects`, `get_tasks`, `get_leads`, `get_contacts`
- **Write:** `create_task`, `update_task`, `create_idea`, `create_lead`, `update_lead`, `create_contact`, `create_note`, `create_contact_note`, `log_deal_activity`

Loop: model call → execute tool calls via the existing `executeAITool(name, args, userId)` → feed results back → repeat (cap at ~6 iterations). The system prompt carries the triage rubric:

```
You are {firstName}'s Chief of Staff. Rules:
1. SEARCH BEFORE CREATE — always search_across_all / get_leads first;
   if the entity exists, update it (append to notes) instead of duplicating.
2. Capture bar: commitments with a who/what → task. New person with
   business potential → lead; personal → contact. Money mentioned on an
   existing deal → log_deal_activity. Novel business idea → idea.
   Durable fact ("my passport expires March") → note.
3. Do NOT capture: small talk, questions, transient logistics,
   anything already in the system.
4. Every write must map to specific words the user said — include that
   excerpt in your final summary.
5. When unsure (significance 0.4–0.7), PROPOSE instead of writing.
```

User context injection: the `users` doc already has `bio`, `role`, `industry`, `goals`, `businesses` — same enrichment the lead-strategy feature does. That's what makes it *his* chief of staff rather than a generic extractor.

**Stage 3 — reply + record captures.** Final model output is the conversational reply plus a structured capture summary. Persist each capture as an **`aiInsights` row — no new collection needed**:

| aiInsights field | CoS usage |
|---|---|
| `category` | `"cos_capture"` (new value — field is free-text, no migration) |
| `priority` | derived from significance |
| `title` / `content` | capture title / source excerpt + what was written |
| `actionType` | `"cos_created"` \| `"cos_proposed"` |
| `actionData` | `{ conversationId, significance, toolCall }` — for proposed: the exact pending `executeAITool` args |
| `relatedEntityType` / `relatedEntityId` | the created entity |
| `isActioned` / `isDismissed` | confirm / dismiss state |

The confirm endpoint for a *proposed* capture just replays `executeAITool(actionData.toolCall.name, actionData.toolCall.args, userId)` and stamps `relatedEntityId`. The web review inbox becomes a filtered view (`category == "cos_capture"`) on infrastructure that already renders insights.

### The significance dial (the product's soul)

```
≥ 0.7  → auto-execute, report in reply           ("logged it")
0.4–0.7 → propose (aiInsights pending, no write)  ("want me to log it?")
< 0.4  → nothing                                  (just converse)
```

Start thresholds conservative (auto-execute sparingly); dismissed captures are training data — later you can inject "recent dismissals" into the Stage-2 prompt as few-shot negative examples, which is how the CoS learns *his* bar for "important" without any fine-tuning.

### Conversation memory

Reuse the existing `conversations` / `messages` collections (schema.ts:313–337): append user + assistant turns each call, feed the last ~20 into Stage 2. One CoS conversation per day ("Daily log — Jul 27") keeps context windows bounded and gives a natural browsing unit on the web side. `metadata` on messages can carry capture ids so the web UI can show which chat line produced which record.

### Cost sketch (per your existing pricing in the admin dash)

- Gate: Flash on every message — ~$0.0001/msg
- Tool loop: GPT-5 only on the ~20–30% that gate in — a few cents each
- A heavy day (50 msgs, 12 captures) ≈ **$0.30–0.50/day/user** — comfortably inside a pro-tier subscription

---

**Effort estimate:** `chiefOfStaff.ts` is roughly 400–500 lines reusing `executeAITool`, `callOpenAIWithLogging`, `storage`, and `aiInsights` — 2–4 days of focused work including the capture-review endpoints. The mobile app then only needs auth + one endpoint + chip rendering.

Want me to actually build `server/chiefOfStaff.ts` on a branch (`feat/chief-of-staff`) with the endpoints + prompts + a filtered captures view wiring, so you can test it via curl before any mobile work starts?

I was already in the process of building a mobile app, can you take a look and see how we can improve it to fit the idea of having a Chief of Staff in your pocket? 

Here is the repo of the current mobile app build: coolgeekme/disciplined-hustle-pulse
Env var didn't persist — re-exporting:

Took a good look. Honest assessment first, because the answer matters for where we go next: **this repo isn't a mobile app yet, and it's currently a different product than the Chief of Staff vision.** Here's what's actually there:

## What `disciplined-hustle-pulse` is today

- **"Pulse" — a Next.js 15 web app**, single page (`src/app/page.tsx`): enter a task → 25-min focus timer → confetti + random reward → repeat. A "Dopamine Dashboard." Clean, well-scoped, tests included — it's a nice motivational micro-app.
- **No mobile layer** — no React Native, no Expo, no Capacitor. It's a website (installable as a bookmark at best; there's no PWA manifest/service worker either).
- **No backend, no auth, no persistence** — all state is React `useState`; your stats vanish on refresh. Zero connection to DisciplinedOS.
- **No chat or voice** — nothing agent-shaped yet.
- **Stray template code**: `src/components/dashboard/` + `src/lib/mock-data.ts` are a *tennis clinic* dashboard (lessons, courts, clinics, player activity) on mock data — looks like leftovers from a template or another project. Dead weight; nothing imports mock-data except those components, and `page.tsx` doesn't render them.

So the gap to "Chief of Staff in your pocket" isn't an improvement list — it's a re-founding of the app around a different core loop, keeping Pulse as a feature.

## How I'd reshape it

**1. The core loop flips: chat is home, not the timer.** A CoS app opens to a conversation ("What's up, boss?" + today's 3 priorities pulled from DisciplinedOS), with a persistent mic button. Pulse's focus timer becomes a *tab* — and it gets better in the process, because "Lock in for 25 minutes on **Fix Eva's checkout page**" can pull real tasks from DisciplinedOS instead of free-typed text, and completed sessions can write back (task → done, hustle score credit). The dopamine loop stays; it just gets real data.

**2. The platform decision — you have three routes:**

| Route | What it gets you | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Expo/React Native rewrite (my rec)** | True App Store/Play Store app, native mic + push-to-talk, push notifications ("I logged 3 things today"), background audio | Rewrite the UI (~small — Pulse is ~6 components), but the right foundation |
| B. Capacitor-wrap this Next.js app | In stores fast, one codebase | Voice UX is second-class WebView; push is clunkier; you'd still restructure the UI anyway |
| C. Stay web/PWA | Zero new tooling | Not "in your pocket" — no store presence, iOS PWA voice/push limits kill the CoS feel |

Since the whole premise is voice-first capture anywhere, **A** is the one that fits. The good news: Pulse's components are simple Tailwind/React — porting to Expo (with NativeWind, which is Tailwind for RN) is mostly mechanical, and the rewards logic (`src/lib/rewards.ts`) ports untouched.

**3. Target structure (Expo):**

```
app/
  (tabs)/
    index.tsx        ← CoS chat (home): messages + capture chips + mic
    focus.tsx        ← Pulse, ported: timer + rewards, tasks from DisciplinedOS
    briefing.tsx     ← Today: calendar, priorities, pending captures to confirm
  login.tsx          ← Firebase Auth (same project as DisciplinedOS)
lib/
  api.ts             ← Bearer-token client → /api/cos/message, /api/quick-add, /api/tasks…
  rewards.ts         ← ported as-is from Pulse
components/
  CaptureChip.tsx    ← "📌 Logged: Task — follow up w/ Rogers RV" [view] [undo]
  PushToTalk.tsx     ← hold-to-record → /api/voice-transcribe → /api/cos/message
```

**4. What carries over vs. what goes:**
- ✅ Keep: the brand/visual identity (gold gradient, dark theme), `rewards.ts` + celebration concept, the focus-session loop, the tests' spirit
- ❌ Drop: the entire tennis-clinic `dashboard/` + `mock-data.ts`
- 🔁 Depends on the server: the CoS chat needs the `/api/cos/message` triage endpoint from my earlier sketch to exist in DisciplinedOS — the app is the mouth, the endpoint is the brain. Worth building the endpoint first (testable via curl, usable by the PWA too).

**5. Sequencing that gets you a pocket CoS fastest:**
1. `feat/chief-of-staff` branch on DisciplinedOS — the triage endpoint (~2–4 days, per the earlier sketch)
2. New Expo app (or convert this repo — fresh `apps/` dir, keep git history): auth + chat + text-only capture chips (~1 week)
3. Push-to-talk voice via existing `/api/voice-transcribe` (~2–3 days)
4. Port Pulse in as the Focus tab, wired to real tasks (~2–3 days)
5. Push notifications + morning briefing tab (~1 week)

That's roughly 3–4 weeks part-time to a TestFlight build that genuinely feels like a chief of staff.

# LinkedIn AI News Roundup

Use when the user asks to "post AI news to LinkedIn", "share the latest AI news on LinkedIn", a daily AI-news LinkedIn update, or anything similar.

Two halves:
1. **Research + Write** — fully automatable, runs anywhere (including a scheduled cron). Gathers the last ~24h of AI news, verifies against primary sources, writes a casual no-emoji post.
2. **Publish** — ONLYvia browser automation against the user's OWN logged-in LinkedIn session (the desktop `computer_use` path). Never from the remote Hermes server, which has no user session and would trip bot detection / need credentials. Always pause for human confirmation before the final "Post" click.

Load `social-media-creative-production` alongside this skill for voice/caption rules — its "Voice & News-Roundup Posts" section is authoritative for tone (casual, no jargon, always include "what it means for us", open question to drive comments). Load `hermes-browser-automation` for the in-app `browser_*` tool caveats when using the server browser instead.

## Voice rules (apply every time)
- Casual, non-technical, human-to-friend tone. No jargon dumps.
- **No emojis** in the final post (user explicitly requested this).
- Always lead with the takeaway, then the stories, then an open question to drive comments.
- Include a "what it means for us" angle after each headline (1-2 sentences).
- Two-pass format is welcome: offer a short punchy version + a longer casual version.
- **Verification honesty:** flag any item sourced only from aggregator roundups as "confirm via source first" before publishing. Never present aggregator claims as confirmed fact.

## Part 1 — Research + Write (automatable, runs anywhere)

### Sources to query (fresh each run)
Use `web_search` for discovery and `web_extract` (or the source article) for verification. Prefer primary sources (vendor blogs, TechCrunch, Guardian, Ars Technica, NYT, Reuters) over aggregator roundups.

Good recurring queries:
- `AI news today <today's date>`
- `OpenAI OR Anthropic OR Google OR Meta AI announcement <date>`
- `AI agent autonomous security <recent>`
- `AI model release tracker <date>`

Filter to the **last 24 hours**. If a strong story is ~48h old but is the week's biggest item (e.g. a major model release), include it but label the recency honestly in your verbal summary to the user — NOT by faking the date in the post.

### Post structure
```
<casual hook — 1-2 sentences, the takeaway>

<3 numbered stories, each: 1-line plain-English what happened + "what it means for us" + source links>

<short "what this means for the rest of us" bullet list — 2-4 bullets>

<big-picture 1-2 sentences>

<open question to drive comments>

#hashtags (6-8, no emoji)
```

### Deliverable for draft-only / cron mode
Write the post to a file at `$HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` AND print it in chat. State clearly which items are verified vs flagged-unverified.

## Part 2 — Publish (user's own machine only, human-in-the-loop)

This half runs ONLY when the user is on a machine where Hermes's `computer_use` driver can reach a browser already logged into LinkedIn. From a remote/headless server it cannot work — say so and fall back to draft-only.

### Preconditions to confirm with the user
- "Are you logged into LinkedIn in a browser Hermes can reach on this machine?" If no, stop and deliver the draft for manual paste.
- Never ask for or type LinkedIn credentials. Never attempt `browser_navigate` to a LinkedIn login and fill a password.
- LinkedIn actively fights automation/bot logins. Pre-authentication (user already signed in) is mandatory; bot-detection may still challenge, and the user must handle any 2FA/CAPTCHA.

### Publish flow (computer_use)
1. `computer_use(action="capture", app="<browser>")` — get a screenshot + AX tree. Prefer limiting to the browser app.
2. Navigate to the LinkedIn feed / start-post composer. If not logged in (login wall visible), STOP — do not proceed; deliver draft for manual paste.
3. Open the "Start a post" composer.
4. Type the full post text into the composer textbox (`action="type"`).
5. Verify the text rendered correctly (re-capture, read the composer content).
6. **MANDATORY PAUSE:** do NOT click the final "Post" button. Tell the user the post is composed and waiting, and ask them to review + click Post themselves (or explicitly authorize Hermes to click it). This protects against accidental posts and bot flags.
7. Only after explicit user confirmation may `computer_use` click the Post button — and even then, prefer the user does it.

### Why a human-confirm pause is non-negotiable
- LinkedIn ToS gray/prohibited zone for automated profile posting; silent auto-Post risks account flags/locks.
- Prevents posting a draft with unverified items or a typo.
- The user owns the account; the agent owns the draft.

## Cron wiring (daily automated draft)
Set a daily cron that loads THIS skill + the research half only, delivers the draft to chat. Example prompt for the cron:
"Load skill linkedin-ai-news-roundup. Run Part 1 (research + write) for the last 24h of AI news. Save the post to $HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<today>.md and print it in chat. Do NOT publish — draft only. Casual voice, no emojis, include what-it-means-for-us and source links. Flag any unverified aggregator-sourced items."

Publishing stays a deliberate, user-initiated action (Part 2) on the user's machine.

## Common pitfalls
- Using emojis (user said no).
- Presenting aggregator roundups as verified fact — flag them.
- Trying to publish from the remote server browser (no session, bot-detection, credential risk) — fall back to draft.
- Typing the user's LinkedIn password — never.
- Clicking "Post" without explicit user confirmation.
- Faking a story's date to make it look <24h — be honest about recency in the chat summary.

The user has provided the following instruction alongside the skill invocation: [IMPORTANT: You are running as a scheduled cron job. DELIVERY: Your final response will be automatically delivered to the user — do NOT use send_message or try to deliver the output yourself. Just produce your report/output as your final response and the system handles the rest. SILENT: If there is genuinely nothing new to report, respond with exactly "[SILENT]" (nothing else) to suppress delivery. Never combine [SILENT] with content — either report your findings normally, or say [SILENT] and nothing more.]

Load skill linkedin-ai-news-roundup. Run ONLY Part 1 (research + write) for the last 24 hours of AI news. Save the full post (short + long version + source links + verification notes) to $HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<today>.md.

For the CHAT DELIVERY (what the user sees here), output ONLY the ready-to-post content — the short version and the long version, hashtags, and source links — formatted as a clean copy-paste block with NO explanatory commentary, NO "verification notes" section, NO "draft, not published" boilerplate. End with a one-line note: "✅ Ready to paste into LinkedIn. Reply 'post' and I'll walk you through publishing on your machine."

Casual voice, no emojis, include what-it-means-for-us and source links. Flag any unverified aggregator-sourced items inline in the post (e.g. "(confirm via source)"), but keep the chat output strictly the post itself.

SHORT VERSION

Big weekend in AI. Three things worth knowing:

- `AI agent autonomous security <recent>`

- Prevents posting a draft with unverified items or a typo.

topics.name: Sharing GitHub repo without affecting main

sessions.title: Sharing GitHub repo without affecting main

messages.content: what's the best way for me to share a github repository to someone so they can "play around" with the code and not touch the main codebase?

The cleanest way is a **fork**. Here's the rundown by scenario:

## Best for "play around without touching anything" → Fork
1. They click **Fork** on your repo → it copies to *their* GitHub account.
2. They clone *their* fork, hack away, commit, push — all to their own copy.
3. Your main repo is untouched. They can only affect it if you accept a Pull Request they open (and you control that).

This is ideal because it costs them nothing, needs no permissions from you, and there's zero risk to your codebase. They can delete their fork whenever.

## Other options, ranked

| Approach | When it's right | Risk to main repo |
|---|---|---|
| **Fork** | Most "play around" cases | None — separate copy |
| **Add as collaborator + branch** | They're a trusted teammate on a shared project | Low, but they *can* push branches/PRs to your repo |
| **GitHub Codespace (fork)** | You want them to run it in-browser, no local setup | None if launched from their fork |
| **Template repo** (`Use this template`) | They want to spin up their *own* new project from your code | None — makes a fresh standalone repo |
| **Local clone, no push** | They just want to read/run it locally; you don't even need their GitHub | None — stays on their machine |

## Quick recommendation
- **Casual tinkering / learning the code** → Fork (or just clone locally if they don't need to save changes back to GitHub).
- **They might contribute later** → Fork + they open a PR when ready.
- **Zero setup, runs in the cloud** → Have them fork, then launch a Codespace from the fork.
- **Starting something new based on your code** → Mark it as a **template repo** so they hit "Use this template."

One thing to watch: if your repo has secrets (`.env`, API keys) committed, forking exposes them to the fork owner. Use `.gitignore` + rotate any exposed credentials before sharing.

Want me to walk through the exact fork-and-Codespace steps, or are you sharing one of your brand repos specifically?
can i create the fork and share that? the current repo is private

Short answer: **No** — forking a private repo won't do what you want.

Here's the catch: when you fork a **private** repo, the fork inherits private visibility and is only visible to people who already have access to the original. So you can't use a fork to grant access to someone new — if they couldn't see your repo before, they can't see the fork either.

## To share a private repo, do this instead

**Add them as a collaborator (best option):**
1. On the repo → **Settings → Collaborators (or "Access") → Invite a collaborator**
2. Enter their GitHub username/email, give them **Write** (or Read if they only need to explore)
3. They get their own clone, can branch freely, and submit changes via **Pull Request**

To make sure they **can't touch `main`**:
- **Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule** for `main`
- Check **"Require a pull request before merging"** and **"Require approvals"**
- Now even with Write access, they can't push directly to `main` — everything goes through a PR you review.

## Other paths
| Goal | Approach |
|---|---|
| Keep it private, let them tinker + contribute | Add collaborator (Write) + protect `main` |
| Keep it private, read-only exploration | Add collaborator with **Read** access |
| They just want to run/read locally, no GitHub needed | Give them a local clone or a `.zip` download — zero risk |
| Open it up fully | Change repo visibility to **Public** (then forking works, but it's now public) |
| Many people, structured access | Move repo into a **GitHub Org** with teams |

One caution: if your repo has any **secrets committed** (`.env`, keys, tokens), adding a collaborator exposes those to them — use `.gitignore` and rotate anything sensitive before inviting.

Short answer: **No — Hermes doesn't have a Chrome extension**, and what it does have works differently from the "Claude for Chrome" model you're thinking of. Let me clear up exactly what each does:

## What Claude/Codex do (the extension model)
"Claude for Chrome" (Anthropic's preview extension) installs into *your* Chrome and lets Claude act inside *your actual browser* — your logged-in sessions, cookies, tabs. That's a local-extension trust model. Codex doesn't really have that; it runs in a cloud sandbox.

## What Hermes has
Hermes ships a **browser toolset** (`browser_navigate`, `browser_click`, etc.), but it's **backend-side and headless**:

- It's driven by the `agent-browser` CLI, which spins up a **fresh headless Chromium** on whatever machine the backend runs on — in your case, the **VPS**, not your laptop.
- It is **not** your real Chrome. It doesn't see your cookies, passwords, logged-in sessions, or open tabs. Every visit starts from a clean slate.
- It can still do real web tasks: navigate, fill forms, click through OAuth consent screens, screenshot, read the page. But it's "an isolated browser," not "your browser."

So there is **no Hermes Chrome extension** that would let me reach into your personal browser on your Windows machine the way the Claude extension does.

## Your realistic options

| What you want | How |
|---|---|
| Agent drives a browser **on the VPS** (no your-sessions access) | Install `agent-browser` on the VPS — already documented, works today |
| Agent drives a browser **on your laptop** (local, separate from your Chrome) | Run the Hermes desktop backend **locally** on Windows with `agent-browser` installed — it'd drive a local headless Chromium |
| Agent controls **your actual Chrome** with your logins | ❌ Not available — no extension ships, and this is a meaningful trust boundary (an extension that hands an AI full control of your authenticated browser) |

One honest caveat: even a local headless instance won't carry *your* Chrome profile/cookies. If the goal is "log into my Instagram/Google from the agent," the cleaner path Hermes already has is the **Instagram MCP** (for IG posting) and the OAuth flows the browser tool can walk through — not a full browser-takeover extension.

Hermes doesn't ship its own proprietary app-store app — it's a gateway bot that you reach **through** existing messaging/UI apps. Based on the actual platform adapters in this repo (27+ supported), here are the best mobile access paths, ranked by popularity and how well they work on a phone:

## 1. Messaging apps (the main mobile path)
You connect Hermes as a bot and chat with it from the app you already have. The most popular ones with first-class mobile apps:

| App | Adapter in repo | Mobile fit |
|-----|------|-----------|
| **Telegram** | `plugins/platforms/telegram` | ✅ Best all-round — clean bot API, rich mobile app, buttons, voice |
| **Discord** | `plugins/platforms/discord` | ✅ Great if you already use it; servers + DMs |
| **WhatsApp** | `whatsapp.py` / `whatsapp_cloud.py` | ✅ Cloud API or Baileys bridge |
| **Signal** | `plugins/platforms/signal` | ✅ Privacy-first |
| **Matrix** (Element app) | `plugins/platforms/matrix` | ✅ Decentralized, excellent mobile client |
| **Slack** | `plugins/platforms/slack` | ✅ If you live in Slack |
| **LINE** | `plugins/platforms/line` | ✅ Popular in Asia |
| **BlueBubbles** | `gateway/platforms/bluebubbles` | ✅ iMessage on iPhone |
| **WeChat/Weixin, Feishu/Lark, DingTalk, QQ, Teams, Google Chat, Mattermost, SMS, ntfy, SimpleX** | various | Region/work-specific |

For a private, low-friction setup (which fits what you've done before), **Telegram is the community default** — it has the cleanest bot setup, a native mobile app on every platform, and support for slash commands, buttons, and voice messages out of the box.

## 2. Web dashboard in a mobile browser
`hermes dashboard` serves a browser UI, and the repo even has `web/src/lib/pty-mobile-input.ts` — meaning the dashboard is built to accept input from a phone browser. Not an app, but bookmarks to your server's URL on your home screen give an app-like experience.

## 3. Third-party AI-chat apps via the API server
Hermes exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API endpoint** (`hermes ... api-server`). You can point any OpenAI-compatible mobile client at it — **Open WebUI, LobeChat, LibreChat, ChatBox** all have mobile apps and can use Hermes as the backend with its full toolset.

## 4. Run Hermes directly on Android (Termux)
There's a `getting-started/termux.md` guide — you can run the agent itself on an Android phone, no server needed.

## Which should you pick?
- **Easiest, most popular:** Telegram bot → chat from the Telegram app.
- **Most private / no cloud:** Matrix (Element) or Signal.
- **Want a ChatGPT-style UI on your phone:** connect ChatBox/LobeChat to the Hermes API server.
- **Already self-hosting:** bookmark the `hermes dashboard` URL on your phone.

Short answer: **no — the VPS vs. laptop distinction is exactly why Desktop app is the right choice, and it makes no difference to the auth flow.** Let me explain why, because it's a common point of confusion.

## What actually matters for OAuth here

The OAuth "application type" (Desktop vs Web) is **only about how the authorization code gets back to Hermes** — it does *not* care where the code runs. The flow is:

1. Hermes (on your VPS) generates an auth URL and gives it to **you**.
2. **You** open that URL in a browser **on your laptop** and approve.
3. Google redirects your laptop's browser to `http://localhost:1?code=...` — which fails to load (expected), so **you copy the URL from the address bar** and paste it back to me.
4. Hermes (on the VPS) exchanges that code for a token.

Notice: at no point does anything need to *connect* to your VPS from Google or from your browser. The "redirect" never actually completes a network connection — it just puts the code in your address bar for you to copy. That's why **Desktop app** (which uses a `localhost` loopback redirect) works perfectly even though Hermes is on a remote server.

## Why Desktop app is correct here (not Web)

| | Desktop app | Web application |
|---|---|---|
| Needs a publicly reachable server? | **No** | Yes (Google pings your redirect URI) |
| Needs you to fill JavaScript origins / redirect URIs? | **No** | Yes |
| Works with Hermes on a headless VPS? | **Yes** (code copied manually) | Awkward — Google would try to reach `localhost` *on your laptop*, not the VPS |

A "Web application" type is for when Google must actually call back a real, internet-facing URL (like `https://myapp.com/oauth/callback`). Your VPS isn't serving a public OAuth callback endpoint, so Web type would be the wrong fit and force you to configure URIs that don't correspond to anything real.

## So:
- **Create it as Desktop app.** VPS location is irrelevant — the manual "copy the code from the address bar" step is what bridges your laptop to the VPS, and Desktop app is built for exactly that.
- The skill is hardcoded for this: it uses `http://localhost:1` as the redirect and reads the code you paste. No server-side listener needed.
